title: EXCLUSIVE: Perez Hilton Trims $350K From Price of Las Vegas Mansion—As Family Begs Fans to Vacate Miami Home Where Health Incident Occurred
author: Kelsi Karruli
preview: The 48-year-old media personality initially listed the six-bedroom, 6.5-bathroom property for $4.25 million in June.
summary_raw: The 48-year-old media personality initially listed the six-bedroom, 6.5-bathroom property for $4.25 million in June.
content_encoded_raw:
Celebrity blogger Perez Hilton has reduced the asking price of his sprawling Las Vegas mansion by $350,000—nearly one month after he was hospitalized following a health incident at his new Miami home.

The 48-year-old media personality initially listed the six-bedroom, 6.5-bathroom property for $4.25 million in June, telling Realtor.com® at the time that the custom-built residence had "served" him well during his years in Nevada.

Now, Hilton has reduced the price to $3.9 million as he looks to sever his remaining real estate ties to Nevada and settle permanently in Miami with his three children and mother.

The price cut comes mere hours after his family issued a public plea on his website asking fans and onlookers to stop gathering around his Miami residence—following a distressing livestream that prompted several calls to police and requests for a welfare check.

Officers ultimately transported Hilton to a nearby hospital, while mental health professionals and the Crisis Response Unit offered support to his friends and family.

The message revealed that before the livestream event, Hilton's "children, niece, and sister were inside the home."

"When it became clear that Perez was experiencing a severe mental health crisis and harming himself, they immediately fled to protect the children from witnessing any further trauma," the message continued.

The update said the family's priority is now "helping the children begin to heal from what they experienced," while explaining that allowing them to return to the privacy and familiarity of their home is an important part of that process.

Hilton's family previously revealed that he was receiving medical care and was "able to communicate."

The update came after Hilton opened about his move to Realtor.com, reflecting on what he'll miss most about his property and his fond memories of Las Vegas.

“It is a beautiful home, and it served me well personally and professionally," he said. "I filmed tons of television segments and news interviews from this home, and produced two documentaries.

"I would film every day for my socials, and livestream as well, and I do a lot of talking head commentary work. I filmed tons of specials for different networks and streamers in my home and outdoors. It's just so beautiful,"

"All three of my favorite spaces in the home have one thing in common—they are all very healing for me. The primary bath has the biggest, most luxurious shower that I've ever had, and the closet is huge and has so much space. Also, I never had my own, dedicated office before, and I really loved that. It's just the perfect home for a family. Everybody has space," he added.

Speaking about the property's location, Hilton told Realtor.com, "It was important for me to be close to the Strip, but it’s equal distance to Summerlin and everywhere we needed to be. My children’s schools, doctors, and dentists were all just a few minutes away.”

Hilton was especially pleased with the fact that his mother had her own private living space. One of home designer Blue Heron's signature features is a "NexGen Suite," and, because he bought the home before it was finished, he got to customize elements of the layout to ensure they were perfect for his mom.

“This was perfect for me, because my mother is a huge part of my family,” said Hilton. “She’s both grandmother and co-parent to my children. To be able to give her the space that she deserves was important. She had her own entrance, her own living room and kitchenette area."

However, despite his love for Nevada, Hilton noted that he is confident in his decision.

"It just feels like the right move, the only move, to make at this time. I've loved Las Vegas, but it's time to be closer to family," he added.

The property is being sold with Kathryn Winterton of Las Vegas Sotheby’s real estate agency, who told Realtor.com, "This home was designed for the way people want to live and entertain today. The natural light, open spaces, and seamless connection to the backyard create an atmosphere that feels both sophisticated and welcoming."

The home spans 7,000 square feet and boasts several modern living spaces, as well as a resort-style pool.

As in so many family dwellings, Hilton says the kitchen is the heart of the home, with its premium appliances, sleek custom cabinetry and a massive dining and prep island.

The kitchen opens up to the high-ceiling living and dining areas, which feel expansive, welcoming and luxurious. Generous walls of glass provide abundant natural light create a light, airy atmosphere.

Outdoors on the acre lot there's a pool, spa, lush landscaping and multiple outdoor gathering spaces. Hilton said he did a lot of his production work outside, as there are a variety of luxurious backdrops ideal for his commentary.

Set in a chic, private gated neighborhood known as Prado, Hilton enjoyed the fact that the home is on a corner lot in a small community with fewer than 20 homes.

"It's not only super private, but also very intimate," he said.

Hilton and his family enjoyed the home, the community and Las Vegas in general so much he says he feels a bit of guilt moving his family away. But "kids are adaptable," he says. He knows this from experience.

A little over three years ago, Hilton packed up his three children and his mother and moved to Las Vegas from Los Angeles, the city where he had infinite Hollywood connections and a luxe, six bedroom, five bath classic Spanish Colonial built in 1926.

Prior to that, Hilton and his family lived in New York City for several years.

Hilton took to Instagram to explain the reasoning behind his move from Las Vegas, where he has been living for the past 3.5 years.

"We’re moving permanently to Miami. I am so excited, not nervous. I know this is the right move for me and my children and my mother," he said at the beginning of the video.

Although Hilton insisted he has "nothing but wonderful memories" while calling Nevada home, he claimed that his decision to relocate to the Sunshine State came from a higher power.

“I need to move to Miami for many reasons. First, this is heaven-sent. God told me to move to Miami. ... The holy spirit made these words come out of my mouth: ‘Let’s move to Miami,'" he said.

The influencer noted that his "trauma" from growing up in The Magic City has since been "released."

“My entire family is in Miami. I still have friends from high school. Though I have not lived there in 30 years, it has always been my home. Once we move there, any second now, it will feel like home right away," he added.

Hilton, who has three children via surrogacy, said a large part of his decision to move was due to his difficult year, which was filled with several health scares, including a 21-day hospital stay and a blood clot.

"Even though it was really painful being in the hospital and so sick, I reconnected with my faith, and this move to Miami feels divine. I was just listening to God. I used to not have a great relationship with Miami when I was younger, but now things are different and Miami is different, and I'm excited to get to rediscover it as an adult," he told Realtor.com.

Speaking about his health woes, he said, "I know this move will be great for my family. Nearly dying this year twice and the experience here—you never think it’s going to happen, but it was just so hard not only for me but my mom, for the kids, for my sister who is in Los Angeles. Everybody else is in Miami. To a new beginning and thank you, God, for guiding me back to Florida where my family needs to be.”

title: ‘Selling Sunset’ Star Christine Quinn’s Ex Lists $5.5 Million L.A. Home as Bitter Divorce Battle Rages On
author: Kelsi Karruli
preview: The tech entrepreneur purchased the home for $5 million in 2019, the same year he and Quinn tied the knot.
summary_raw: The tech entrepreneur purchased the home for $5 million in 2019, the same year he and Quinn tied the knot.
content_encoded_raw:
"Selling Sunset" star Christine Quinn's husband, Christian Dumontet, has listed the sprawling Los Angeles home the former couple once shared as their contentious divorce battle continues.

Dumontet filed for divorce from the real estate agent—who is set to make her return to the Netflix reality series—in April 2024, after he was arrested following an alleged domestic violence incident. He was later detained for allegedly violating a temporary restraining order requiring him to stay away from the property.

The tech entrepreneur purchased the home for $5 million in 2019, the same year he and Quinn tied the knot in an extravagant Gothic-themed wedding.

However, their relationship ultimately unraveled, with the pair calling it quits in 2024.

Amid their ongoing divorce proceedings, Dumontet asked a judge to grant him exclusive control of the Los Angeles property so he could put it on the market. He argued that he purchased the residence before the couple married and had continued covering its mortgage, taxes, and insurance.

He claimed that neither he nor Quinn—who recently moved back to her home state of Texas—had lived at the property since September 2025, despite the residence still costing him around $27,000 a month.

According to TMZ, Dumontet also claimed that he previously spent $30,000 a month on round-the-clock security for the property and continues to shell out $7,500 a month for a caretaker.

Although the court previously denied his emergency request, the home officially hit the market on Sept. 8 with Josh Flagg of Compass, carrying a $5.49 million asking price.

Built in 2010, the four-bedroom, six-bathroom residence sits above the Sunset Strip and pairs contemporary architecture with sprawling entertaining spaces and resort-style amenities.

The listing describes the gated property as "a sophisticated contemporary retreat above the Sunset Strip," noting its "expressive architecture, substantial scale, and a refined interplay of natural materials and glass."

The residence was previously owned by Crystal Hefner and has appeared in People magazine and several architectural publications, giving it a notable Hollywood pedigree even before Quinn and Dumontet called it home.

Inside, a dramatic entryway gives way to soaring ceilings, walls of glass, and expansive living spaces designed to take advantage of the surrounding skyline views.

The chef's kitchen anchors the home's open-concept layout and features walnut cabinetry, stainless-steel accents, dual ovens, dual dishwashers, and a large center island.

The spacious primary suite offers floor-to-ceiling windows, while its striking bathroom features a large soaking tub set against a dramatic black pebble-stone wall.

But some of the property's most impressive amenities can be found on its lower level, which has been designed almost entirely for entertainment.

There, the next owner will have access to a Dolby Atmos movie theater, lounge, arcade area, refrigerated wine cellar, and bar. There's also an additional en suite bedroom, creating what the listing describes as a "self-contained setting for guests and gatherings."

Outside, the home's resort atmosphere continues with a large swimming pool surrounded by lush landscaping, offering a private retreat just above one of Los Angeles' most famous stretches.

The decision to put their former marital home on the market marks yet another major change for the exes as they continue navigating their divorce, while Quinn prepares to step back into the spotlight with her return to reality TV.

Quinn announced the news of her return in an Instagram video, telling fans she's "back" before asking if they missed her.

Quinn, who took a four-year break from the show, told Tudum that things in the Oppenheim office, which is led by Jason and Brett Oppenheim, will be different this time around, warning fans to expect a "reintroduction" when the season kicks off.

"This isn’t a rewind. It’s a reintroduction," Quinn said, before opening up about how her return to the show first came about.

"Adam DiVello and I reconnected after my divorce, and I really appreciate him extending the invitation to come back on," she shared, referring to the show's creator. "I’m returning from a very different place, with more perspective, confidence, and clarity."

Since leaving the series, Quinn has moved to Texas, previously revealing that she wanted to get back to her roots after her time on the show came to an end.

"A lot of people don't know that I'm actually from Texas originally. So I grew up here, and I went to Southlake Carroll. A lot of people don't know that," she said. "My family still lives in the same house that I grew up in, and I live in the area. I'm a suburb gal.

"Dallas is like my home and Fort Worth as well," she told the Dallas Morning News.

It is unclear what her return to "Selling Sunset" means for her life in the Lone Star State.

Quinn—who was portrayed as the villain during her time on the show—also revealed that becoming a mom has helped her become more "protective of her peace."

“Motherhood has a way of sharpening your priorities and changing how you move through the world. I’ve become more intentional and much more protective of my peace," she said.

However, Quinn assured fans she's still her cutthroat self.

"I’m still ambitious and direct, but I think people will see a version of me that’s more centered and even more sure of herself. I’m hoping this chapter feels fresh and honest. I’m not coming back to play an old version of myself. I’m coming back to show where I am now and let the audience see that growth can still come with an edge," she explained.

title: This $1.25M Mulholland Drive ‘Mansion’ Has No Kitchen, No Sewer—and a Squatter Problem
author: Julie Gerstein
preview: The home at 7711 Mulholland has the makings of a luxury property, but it appears no one ever moved in.
summary_raw: The home at 7711 Mulholland has the makings of a luxury property, but it appears no one ever moved in.
content_encoded_raw:
A home on storied Mulholland Drive in Los Angeles has been left abandoned, and irate neighbors say that squatters and trespassers have taken over.

The home at 7711 Mulholland sits high along a ridge in the East Laurelwood neighborhood of the city and offers panoramic views of the city. It has the makings of a luxury property, but it appears no one ever moved in.

Neighbors said the lot has been taken over by trespassers who are using the half-finished home as a party location.

“The house on the top of the hill has been an issue for a while,” Paul Stern, who lives nearby, told NBC Los Angeles. “Since the point when it was constructed, it wasn't constructed properly. It created a lot of mudslides. We dealt with the mudslides.”

Neighbors said they're sick of dealing with it, and they are growing increasingly concerned about the structural safety of the property.

They've have asked that the city's mayor, Karen Bass, and Councilmember Nithya Rama, who represents the district, intervene. Bass intervened in a similar situation in August, after a fire broke out in an abandoned property in Studio City.

The mayor, who is up for reelection and running against Rama, called for legal action against the Studio City owner after the L.A. Department of Building and Safety (LADBS) called the address a "present, imminent, extreme, and immediate hazard."

Graffiti is visible on the roof of the home as seen from the road, and a city contractor says fresh trash and bottles around the property are indications of recent activity there, according to the Los Angeles Times.

Realtor.com® has reached out to Bass and Rama for comment.

A house, but not a home

The history of 7711 Mulholland is somewhat murky. It was purchased by a company called Walking Media Inc. in 2022 for $1.25 million, seemingly a steal compared to other homes in the area, many of which are listed for double that or more.

But it turns out, the house was only half-finished at the time of the sale.

When it was listed in 2022, it was accompanied by a video tour that showed an expansive hillside home replete with floor-to-ceiling windows, polished concrete floors, and exposed beams. But images of the home's kitchen and bathrooms were conspicuously absent.

That's because, at the moment, they don't exist. When it was last sold, the home had no kitchen, no sewer connection, and no certificate of occupancy. It also lacked a driveway or off-street parking.

Listings described the property as a "development opportunity" requiring "extensive work" to finish.

It's possible that some of that work might begin soon. In May, the owner filed a request for and was issued a building permit and certificate of occupancy with the LADBS.

Yet, since then, two nuisance complaints have been issued against the property and are being investigated by the city.

"Once a conspicuous property appears vacant for an extended period, vandalism, graffiti, trespassing, and exposure to the elements can make an already difficult redevelopment project even much more expensive," says Amo Realty president Daniel Amodeo. Amodeo serves real estate clients throughout the Los Angeles market.

"Buyers for these properties are potentially dealing with engineering, permitting, access, utilities, fire requirements, insurance, and also substantial construction costs before anyone can actually occupy the property," he says. "A buyer can purchase what looks like a really incredible piece of prime L.A. real estate with amazing views and then discover that completing it is a much larger undertaking than buying it."

Surprisingly, 7711 Mulholland isn't the only abandoned mansion in the city. A search of nuisance properties in L.A. uncovered a dozen properties last sold for over $1 million that are either abandoned or unfinished.

Perhaps the most famous of those properties is a $6.5 million Mulholland Drive mansion once owned by John Powers Middleton, erstwhile producer and son of Philadelphia Phillies owner John Middleton.

That property and another owned by Middleton sat fallow for more than a decade, and were overtaken by a group of squatters and grafitti writers.

In 2024, Middleton issued an apology to his neighbors, saying: “What’s happened to the two properties I own is unacceptable. No matter what caused it, I own the houses.”

This article was originally published on Sept. 4, 2026, and was updated with new photos of the Mulholland Drive home on Sept. 10.

(Clint Brewer Photography / BACKGRID) They've have asked that the city's mayor, Karen Bass , and Councilmember Nithya Rama , who represents the district, intervene. Bass intervened in a similar situation in August, after a fire broke out in an abandoned property in Studio City. The mayor, who is up for reelection and running against Rama, called for legal action against the Studio City owner after the L.A. Department of Building and Safety (LADBS) called the address a "present, imminent, extreme, and immediate hazard." Graffiti is visible on the roof of the home as seen from the road, and a city contractor says fresh trash and bottles around the property are indications of recent activity there, according to the Los Angeles Times . Realtor.com® has reached out to Bass and Rama for comment. A house, but not a home The history of 7711 Mulholland is somewhat murky. It was purchased by a company called Walking Media Inc. in 2022 for $1.25 million, seemingly a steal compared to other homes in the area, many of which are listed for double that or more. But it turns out, the house was only half-finished at the time of the sale. When it was listed in 2022, it was accompanied by a video tour that showed an expansive hillside home replete with floor-to-ceiling windows, polished concrete floors, and exposed beams. But images of the home's kitchen and bathrooms were conspicuously absent. That's because, at the moment, they don't exist. When it was last sold, the home had no kitchen, no sewer connection, and no certificate of occupancy. It also lacked a driveway or off-street parking. The hillside home has the makings of a luxury property, but it appears no one ever moved in. (Clint Brewer Photography / BACKGRID) Graffiti and trash on the property provide signs that it has been taken over by squatters and trespassers. (Clint Brewer Photography / BACKGRID) Trash and debris are spread on the hill below the home, causing consternation among neighbors. (Clint Brewer Photography / BACKGRID) Listings described the property as a "development opportunity" requiring "extensive work" to finish. It's possible that some of that work might begin soon. In May, the owner filed a request for and was issued a building permit and certificate of occupancy with the LADBS. Yet, since then, two nuisance complaints have been issued against the property and are being investigated by the city. "Once a conspicuous property appears vacant for an extended period, vandalism, graffiti, trespassing, and exposure to the elements can make an already difficult redevelopment project even much more expensive," says Amo Realty president Daniel Amodeo . Amodeo serves real estate clients throughout the Los Angeles market. "Buyers for these properties are potentially dealing with engineering, permitting, access, utilities, fire requirements, insurance, and also substantial construction costs before anyone can actually occupy the property," he says. "A buyer can purchase what looks like a really incredible piece of prime L.A. real estate with amazing views and then discover that completing it is a much larger undertaking than buying it." The owner of the home is a Delaware-based company called Walking Media Inc., whose owner remains unidentified. (Clint Brewer Photography / BACKGRID) Surprisingly, 7711 Mulholland isn't the only abandoned mansion in the city. A search of nuisance properties in L.A. uncovered a dozen properties last sold for over $1 million that are either abandoned or unfinished. Perhaps the most famous of those properties is a $6.5 million Mulholland Drive mansion once owned by John Powers Middleton , erstwhile producer and son of Philadelphia Phillies owner John Middleton . That property and another owned by Middleton sat fallow for more than a decade, and were overtaken by a group of squatters and grafitti writers. In 2024, Middleton issued an apology to his neighbors, saying: “What’s happened to the two properties I own is unacceptable. No matter what caused it, I own the houses.” This article was originally published on Sept. 4, 2026, and was updated with new photos of the Mulholland Drive home on Sept. 10.

title: Where the Top 1% of Luxury Real Estate Rules the Market
author: Kiri Blakeley
preview: In select markets, the gap between entry-level luxury and the highest luxury tier, ultraluxury, is many multiples.
summary_raw: In select markets, the gap between entry-level luxury and the highest luxury tier, ultraluxury, is many multiples.
content_encoded_raw:
There's luxury and then there's ultraluxury—and, depending on location, the price difference between them can be extreme.

Nationally, ultraluxury listings (which Realtor.com defines as the most expensive 1% of listings) begin at $5.16 million, which is 4.3 times the median $1.20 million entry luxury threshold, or the most expensive 10% of listings in the country.

But in certain markets, that gap widens considerably.

Take Hilo-Kailua on the island of Hawaii, often called the Big Island. The micropolitan area covers all of Hawaii County, but the two areas sit on opposite coasts. Hilo is to the east, and Kailua to the west.

In Hilo-Kailua, entry-level luxury starts at a median of $1,995,000. But the uber-wealthy snapping up the top 1% of properties are able to plunk down 6.2 times that, the steepest gap between entry and ultra in the country.

There is also a bit of a price difference between the two coastal towns.

"Hilo anchors homes that are relatively more affordable," writes Realtor.com® senior economist Anthony Smith in his August 2026 luxury report. "A larger share of high-end inventory sits on the opposite coast, concentrated in the Kamuela area along the South Kohala shoreline, where resort communities hold much of the island's oceanfront estate stock."

Here, he says, exclusive properties with sunset ocean views and private beach access can easily top $20 million. Currently, the priciest listing is a 30-year-old 7,844-square-foot estate on 1.38 acres on the Kohala Coast. The price tag: $29 million.

The Lucky Bennett–designed home with sweeping ocean, fairway, and mountain views comes with a $1,472 HOA fee. It has been on the market for around 200 days and received a $3 million shave. Homes at the luxury level generally sit longer due to the smaller buyer pool, with million-dollar-plus dwellings taking a median of 89 days to move in this Big Island market.

Hilo-Kailua also has one of the lowest inventory levels in the country, with just 1,387 home listings—the third-smallest selection behind Key West–Key Largo, FL, and the Vero Beach metro. These smaller markets tend to be highly susceptible to price fluctuations at the luxury end, especially the top 1%.

"Measuring the top 1% comes with a caveat," explains Smith. The ultraluxury segment is "an incredibly small portion of the overall market, and those listings carry volatility from rare trophy properties, custom homes, and pricing variables that have few comparisons, if any."

This is compounded in markets with fewer than 5,000 total listings, such as Hilo-Kailua. In other words, one or two outliers with extremely high multimillion-dollar price tags can skew the data.

However, those top-tier segments showcase "interesting markets" that prove the highest levels of luxury can extend far beyond the big three of New York City, Miami, and Los Angeles—and can reach into unexpected locations.

Reno's surprising ultraluxury market

Take Reno, NV, for instance.

The city is No. 5 on the list, which ranks the metros with the largest gaps between the top 10% and top 1% of listings, just behind larger markets such as Miami (No. 2), Los Angeles (No. 3), and Port St. Lucie, FL (No. 4).

"Reno is another market on this list that doesn’t enter the luxury conversation often," says Smith.

Reno is small, with only 1,493 listings over the million-dollar price point. Compare that to Miami's 40,908, which is the largest on the list.

Thanks to Reno's slim luxury inventory, these listings sell fast—in a median of only 76 days, far below Miami's 96 days.

And the gap between what the wealthy and the super wealthy can afford is wide. Here, entry-level luxury starts at $1,999,999, not far above the national median of $1.2 million.

But the top 1% starts at a jaw-dropping $10,851,000, a multiple of 5.4 over Reno's entry-level threshold, for the fifth-widest gap on the list.

Currently, the most expensive listing in Reno is the Pennington Mansion, a $13.95 million estate on 14 acres located "in the heart of the small city.

"Properties of this scale simply do not exist this close to town," says the listing. Perched on a "high plateau," the house delivers dazzling skyline and valley views, combined with all the luxury one would expect at this level, including 19,000-plus square feet of living space, a wine cellar and billiard room, large gym, private theater, eight-car garage, and pool and spa.

In general, however, the top-tier ultraluxe properties can be found along Lake Tahoe in Washoe County, especially in the exclusive lakefront communities of Incline Village and Crystal Bay.

"The result is a market that combines a moderately priced valley luxury with a trophy shoreline under one metro," says Smith.

The priciest listing in Lake Tahoe flicks Pennington Mansion off the map: a $47.5 million abode along Lakeshore Boulevard in Incline Village.

Built in in 1975 and spanning a relatively modest 4,530 square feet, this home sits on a little under 2 acres. But what shoots this price tag into the stratosphere is its coveted flat, sandy beach on 106 feet of Crystal Bay lake frontage.

Kerry Donovan of Donovan Group Luxury Sales says prices in Incline Village—long nicknamed "Income Village" for its affluent denizens—skyrocketed after billionaire Silicon Valley venture capitalist Steve Jurvetson, an early investor in Skype, Tesla, and SpaceX, purchased an Incline Village home for $46 million in early 2026.

Then, a month later, he reportedly snapped up an off-market lakefront property for a mind-boggling $125 million. The second sale annihilated the previous record of $62 million paid in 2024 for an Incline Village estate built by casino mogul Steve Wynn.

"It was a beautiful, newer estate property," Donovan tells Realtor.com of the $125 million house. "It was obviously a product that the buyer wanted, and he offered the sellers a price that was good for them to say 'OK.'

"Some of the sales earlier this year defied logical pricing," she adds. Outlier sales such as these threw the local market into what she terms "make me move" pricing.

Spurred on by "make me move" optimism, families who owned properties in the area for generations decided to try their luck with nose-bleed prices in the tens of millions.

The broker says the typical buyer at this level is either a local who is "moving up," or migrants from other tax-friendly states such as Texas, Arizona, and Florida, or uber-wealthy Californians fleeing the "billionaire tax," which will be on the ballot in November.

Nevada, which has no state income tax, no inheritance tax, and comparatively low property taxes, is popular with high net worth individuals looking to shield some of their assets from Uncle Sam, and is drawing buyers from higher-taxed shores such as San Jose and Los Angeles.

"We're seeing a lot more families from Northern California," says the agent. "That's been a big change."

According to Realtor.com data, those with the Reno jones tend to hail from the San Jose-Sunnyvale-Santa Clara metro, with 19.5% of listings views originating in that market, followed by Sacramento-Roseville-Folsom (9%) and Los Angeles (7.8%).

Donovan, who currently represents a $21 million cabin in Incline Village, says buyers are lured by the village's excellent school system—both public and private—as well as its small-town feel combined with its high-end amenities such as skate, BMX, and pickleball courts.

She also notes the easy access to Reno-Tahoe International Airport and Truckee Tahoe private airport, giving Silicon Alley techies flush with AI equity a quick 45-minute flight to another world—one that is quiet, safe, and filled with pristine nature.

Ranked fourth on the list, behind Los Angeles and Miami, is another unexpected and smaller market, this one with only 4,006 listings: Port St. Lucie in the Sunshine State.

Here, $1,099,578 buys an entry into luxury, but a buyer must jump a multiple of 5.4 to reach the ultraluxury threshold, with its median of $6,159,000.

title: Nicole Kidman Reveals She’s Owned a ‘Stealth’ Home in London for 21 Years—and Hints at Plans To Spend Time Abroad After Keith Urban Divorce
author: Hannah Chambers
preview: The "Practical Magic" actress revealed she's secretly held onto an apartment in England for over 20 years.
summary_raw: The "Practical Magic" actress revealed she's secretly held onto an apartment in England for over 20 years.
content_encoded_raw:
Actress Nicole Kidman has major plans to spend more time in London moving forward—though, as the “Nine Perfect Strangers” star has revealed, the city has quietly been a part of her life for decades.

Nearly a year after her split from husband Keith Urban, 58, Kidman, 59, let slip to British Vogue that she’s had an apartment near Notting Hill for quite some time.

“I’ve had it for 20 years … 21 actually,” the actress, who admitted that she has been "lonely" at home following her divorce," said.

It marks the first time that the "Moulin Rouge!" actress has confirmed she owns property in London—having already amassed homes in Beverly Hills, CA; New York City; Nashville, TN; and Australia. While all of those properties have appeared in numerous headlines, her U.K. abode has remained surprisingly under the radar.

“I’m stealth,” Kidman shared of her ability to keep the property so tightly under wraps.

Although she has kept tight-lipped about her property portfolio, Kidman has been open about how her split from Urban has impacted her.

While speaking on the "Therapuss" podcast with host Jake Shane, Kidman admitted that it wasn't until the night she won an Oscar that she realized she didn't have someone to share the wonderful news with.

“I was beyond lonely. I had the pinnacle of my success, and I went home and was so lonely," she said.

“So, yeah, crazy, though, that sort of the confluence of events where you go, ‘I wish…’ I had my mom with me and my dad, but I was like, ‘Where’s my partner, someone that I can share this with?’" Kidman said.

“It was one of the most profound moments where I went, ‘I’ve got to get a life’ and at the same time, I’m holding this gold statue where you go, ‘This is, this is it. This is the highest sort of prize you can get in our industry.’ And so grateful and yet so lonely," she added.

It came as a surprise to fans who have seen the actress seemingly thriving during her "Euro summer," during which she has spent time bouncing between London, Ibiza, Paris, and Portofino, leveraging glasses and a “little dark wig” to conceal her identity when the night whisks her away to the club for some raving.

“I’m good at slipping in and slipping out of everywhere,” she joked.

In the first summer since the separation, Kidman is embracing the unknown, describing the current transitional vibe of her life as “free falling” or “jumping off.”

“Like, where am I going?” she mused. “And what’s next?”

A return to London could certainly be on the list of upcoming adventures for Kidman, who hinted that she is eager to return to the city in order to throw herself into the theater scene.

She remarked that she’d “love to” return to the stage in the British capital, with the outlet noting that she does already own the rights to a handful of plays she’d like to add to her extensive repertoire.

Though she did not elaborate any further on those plans, her eagerness to throw herself into the theatrical mix in London was enough for the Vogue writer to note: "But let it be known, London: she’s coming."

The actress certainly seems settled in the city—taking full advantage of London's thriving theatre industry, alongside her lookalike daughters, Sunday Rose, 18, and Faith Margaret, 15. She explained that the trio has recently crossed a handful of must-see productions off their bucket list in the city’s theatre scene. Recent favorites include “1536,” “The Guilty,” and “The Oresteia.”

Sunday and Faith have also happily been exploring London by themselves; while Kidman completed her cover story interview, her girls—who have become fashion icons in their own right—visited a Schiaparelli exhibit at the Victoria and Albert Museum.

Indeed, the family has had ample time to embrace a European lifestyle in the past 12 months.

Last year, the “Practical Magic” star spent the entire summer in London, shooting the highly anticipated sequel to the iconic film alongside co-star Sandra Bullock. Although the romantic fantasy film takes place in idyllic New England, filming took the cast and crew abroad, and the on-screen sisters spent their spare time making memories in the surrounding areas.

Kidman and Bullock, who are both parents to teens, attended iconic music festival Glastonbury, the Wimbledon tennis tournament, and even a Coldplay concert together.

According to Bullock, the process marked the first time in "decades" that the two women had spent real time together, and both noted that it was a fulfilling experience getting the chance to bring their families together.

Kidman's co-star also opened up about the unique dynamic that exists between the two women, explaining that, though they have incredibly different personalities, their is a bond between them that is very much like that of sisters.

“Nic and I are very different,” the “Miss Congeniality” star divulged to British Vogue. “But our differences create the most fabulous dynamic. Whether we are fighting or loving on each other, we need each other.”

Kidman isn’t the only actor from the iconic witchy film who has decided to lay down roots in the U.K. In 2019, Stockard Channing traded a life in Maine for a change of scenery in London, following the 2014 passing of husband Daniel Gillham.

“The pattern of my life shifted, so I shifted my life from Maine,” Channing explained in a personal essay for The Sunday Times, noting a “lag effect” that resulted in a later realization of just how impactful the loss had been. “I’ve lived alone since I lost Daniel and I’m happy being a recluse.”

The actress will return to the role of Aunt Frances in “Practical Magic 2,” which will premiere on Sept. 11. The cast includes a few new faces, such as Joey King, Lee Pace, and Maisie Williams, but may be the last time Channing graces the screen.

“I’m not sure I’ll do anything after that,” Channing added. “Acting is like everything in life; you never know what’s going to happen.”

As for Kidman, she's showing no signs of slowing down, either personally or professionally, admitting to Vogue that she has been a workaholic since she was just 14 years old and living in Australia.

"I just think there are some people who are wired to work. I just am," she said, adding: "It’s probably from having started work when I was 14."

The actress is understood to travel regularly back to her home country, where she and Urban owned a home together—however, her primary residence is located in Nashville, where she lives with her two teenage daughters.

According to reports, the actress has continued to live in her former marital abode in the wake of her divorce, with sources telling the New York Post in October 2025 that the property was providing Kidman and her daughters with some much needed stability during a time of great upheaval.

"I’m not sure that Nicole will want to remain in Tennessee full time after her children go off to college," the unnamed source said. "But for now, the home will be a source of stability for them while navigating this separation."

Though they bought their property in Nashville for the comparatively low sum of $3.47 million, they are said to have invested plenty of money into turning the palatial dwelling into their dream home.

Kidman and Urban purchased the sprawling estate—which included two adjacent parcels of land—in 2008, according to records, having relocated their family to Nashville the previous year.

Located inside a gated community in Northumberland, the property, which is known as the "Queen of Northumberland," boasts 2 acres, part of which is occupied by a dazzling swimming pool and a large professional tennis court.

The main residence on the property features seven bedrooms and 10 bathrooms, providing more than enough space for Kidman and her daughters.

Other amenities inside the home include a theater, elegant living spaces, and even a "hobby room."

Interestingly, reports about the breakdown of the couple's marriage came just two months after it was revealed that Kidman was eyeing up property in another European locale: Portugal.

According to local media outlet SIC Notícias, the "Practical Magic" star submitted her application to the country’s Agency for Integration, Migration and Asylum in July 2025, with sources telling the publication that she had been looking for a dwelling in the European country for some time.

title: EXCLUSIVE: Steven Spielberg Lists $30 Million L.A. Equestrian Ranch—Decades After Scrapping Controversial 5-Story Riding Ring Plans
author: Kelsi Karruli
preview: Spielberg, 79, and his wife, Kate Capshaw, 72, purchased the property in 1999 through their corporate entity, Texas Tart, for $5.75 million.
summary_raw: Spielberg, 79, and his wife, Kate Capshaw, 72, purchased the property in 1999 through their corporate entity, Texas Tart, for $5.75 million.
content_encoded_raw:
Filmmaker Steven Spielberg has listed the sprawling Los Angeles ranch where he housed his horses for nearly $30 million—decades after abandoning controversial plans to transform the property with an enormous five-story riding facility.

Spielberg, 79, and his wife, Kate Capshaw, 72, purchased the property in 1999 through their corporate entity, Texas Tart, for $5.75 million.

At the time, the Hollywood mogul and actress unveiled ambitious plans to dramatically overhaul the estate with a 27,000-square-foot, five-story riding facility featuring a domed roof and underground horse stables.

Spielberg's vision also reportedly included more than $7 million worth of renovations, as well as plans to construct a 2,400-square-foot guesthouse and a three-story guardhouse.

However, the proposed transformation sparked fierce backlash from neighbors, who objected to the scale of the project.

Although the Oscar-winning director reportedly planned to present revised ideas to his neighbors, the elaborate project ultimately never came to fruition. However, he did get a chance to update the estate into the magnificent abode it is today.

The property remained part of Spielberg and Capshaw's extensive real estate portfolio for nearly three decades.

Now, the couple is finally preparing to part ways with the equestrian retreat, listing it for $29.9 million with Sandro Dazzan of The Agency.

Known as Dogwood, the seven-bedroom, 9.5-bathroom estate sits on 2.8 acres in the ultraprivate Sullivan Canyon and offers an impressive array of equestrian amenities alongside its luxurious living spaces.

"Nestled in the ultra-private Sullivan Canyon, Dogwood is Los Angeles' premiere equestrian ranch - a rare masterpiece designed by renowned architect Michael Kovac with interiors by Michael Smith and landscape design by Christine London," the listing states.

Spanning two parcels, the property combines a sophisticated country-inspired aesthetic with extensive facilities designed for horses, entertaining, and guests.

Inside the main residence, rich walnut floors and wood-covered ceilings create a warm atmosphere, while expansive windows bring in plenty of natural light.

The spacious living room offers multiple seating areas anchored by dual fireplaces, creating an inviting space for relaxing and entertaining.

That rustic aesthetic continues into the chef's kitchen, which features extensive wood cabinetry, an oversized center island, high-end appliances, and an eat-in dining nook.

"The chef's kitchen with eat-in dining nook and wood-burning fireplace connects to a cozy family room and IPE-clad terrace overlooking a tranquil reflection pond," the listing notes.

Upstairs, the primary suite offers a peaceful retreat complete with a wood-burning fireplace and access to a private covered terrace.

The outdoor space boasts yet another fireplace along with sweeping city and canyon views, according to the listing.

Elsewhere inside the home is a media room that can double as a game room, as well as a wine cellar.

But the property's most impressive features are arguably those designed for its four-legged residents.

Across from the main entertaining spaces sits a six-stall barn complete with an executive office, staff quarters, three grooming stations, a feed kitchen, and storage.

The equestrian facility is topped off by a sprawling 20,000-square-foot riding arena with an observation deck and mirrored wall, which the listing notes is suitable for both dressage and jumping.

The estate's lower parcel expands the compound even further with a stylish one-bedroom guesthouse equipped with its own kitchen, rooftop deck, and basement office and storage spaces.

There is also a second four-stall barn, a 5,400-square-foot turnout area, a private gate, and enough parking for more than 10 vehicles.

Both parcels are supported by a security command post and generators, further adding to the property's private compound-like feel.

Outside, the ranch is surrounded by lush landscaping, while a tranquil reflection pond adds to its secluded, countryside atmosphere—despite the estate's location in the heart of Los Angeles.

The $29.9 million listing now marks the end of a decades-long chapter for Spielberg and Capshaw, who held onto the equestrian retreat for nearly 27 years after first purchasing it for a fraction of its current asking price.

Despite having never resided in this property, the couple has plenty of lavish abodes to call home.

Their main residence is a stunning Pacific Palisades abode, which has served as their home since 1985.

The property sprawls across 20,000 square feet and boasts a media room, a 14,000-gallon aquarium, and several other lavish amenities.

Over in Malibu, they own a beachfront abode, which is made up of two parcels.

They purchased the first parcel in 1989 for $3.3 million and picked up the second in 2000 for $3.2 million.

The home is situated on a 1.44-acre lot and boasts 144 feet of ocean frontage.

They also hold the keys to a dwelling in New York, which they purchased in 1983.

The couple snapped up the 6-acre estate and enlisted architect Charles Gwathmey to overhaul the abode.

Over the years, he added horse stables and a lavish guesthouse.

In 2008, he expanded the property by picking up a 3.2-acre pond in the front of the home for $20 million.

Also in the East Coast, the couple also owns a 6,000-square-foot apartment building in Manhattan.

title: The New Housing Law Was Supposed To Help Buyers—Here’s Why Delays Are Coming Instead
author: Tristan Navera
preview: Three months after the most comprehensive housing bill in decades became law, Washington is still getting its bearings on what's next.
summary_raw: Three months after the most comprehensive housing bill in decades became law, Washington is still getting its bearings on what's next.
content_encoded_raw:
Three months after the most comprehensive housing bill in decades became law, the agencies tasked with implementing it are still getting their bearings on what's next.

The 21st Century Road to Housing Act proved a political roller coaster this year as it was closely debated in the House and Senate, breaking multiple deadlocks. Then, President Donald Trump, who initially championed it, stepped back amid other political priorities. But the final passage of the bill laid the groundwork for dozens of new provisions aimed at making it easier to buy a home.

While the bill officially became law 10 days after it was submitted to the White House, it will be some time before some parts of the country see its impacts. And they come at a time when the involved government agencies are seeing cuts in funding.

No one provision of the bill takes effect on its own. It will be up to federal agencies to write new rules and guidance. And some of that could mean new notices and programs that take some time to create.

The bill created about a dozen programs on paper, but they need new funding, which will need to come from future congressional approvals. Because it came after the 2027 House budget, some programs might not receive funding until fiscal year 2028, said Kristen Klurfield, associate director for housing at the Bipartisan Policy Center.

In the meantime, the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development is responsible for 88 of the 125 implementation items. It's also added nine new proposed rules to its agenda. Proposed rulemaking, which is subject to public notice and comment during its formulation, can take 18 to 24 months to finalize.

HUD's seen major staffing cuts, including losing 650 full-time equivalents in the Federal Housing Administration and other housing units, a 27% decrease. Public and Indian Housing has lost 29% of its headcount, or 419 full-time equivalents, according to data from the National Association of Affordable Housing Lenders.

Lesli Gooch, CEO of the Manufactured Housing Institute, laid out the long road ahead. While the federal government updates the building code to address changes to manufactured housing, states need to update their own licensing, zoning, and other laws.

"It means there is time to prepare," said Liz Osborn, vice president of policy at Enterprise Community Partners. "So state and local governments that are looking to take advantage of those opportunities, I would suggest that there's opportunities now to be working in advance to increase housing supply and set themselves up for success."

Hot potato for the midterms

Since the bill's passage, lawmakers have campaigned heavily on the bipartisan nature of the bill as both Democrats and Republicans tighten affordability-focused messages for the midterms.

“Everywhere I go, I hear from families struggling to find housing they can afford," Rep. Jim McGovern (D-MA) said after a round-table with housing advocates on Tuesday at a YMCA in Worcester, MA, nodding to Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-MA), who helped shepherd the bill in the Senate. "I’m grateful to Sen. Warren for her leadership in getting this important legislation passed."

"Committee Republicans have put in the hard work to advance bills strengthening our capital markets, modernizing regulation, expanding housing supply, supporting community financial institutions, and promoting American leadership in financial innovation," Rep. French Hill (R-AR), another of the bill's shepherds, said at a DC hearing last week aimed at lauding the Trump administration's policies.

In doing so, lawmakers have once again taken aim at one another for perceived slowness to act on the affordability metrics. In a letter this month, Warren took aim at Bill Pulte, director of the Federal Housing Finance Agency, for not codifying rules constraining institutional investors in the housing market.

Trump signed an executive order calling for the government to move away from financing housing involving institutional investors. The housing bill added further requirements for that discouraged investor activity.

"While 'Road' takes a strong first step toward returning homeownership opportunities to the American people, there is more that HUD and FHFA can and should do to limit the role of large institutional investors in housing, including in multifamily and manufactured housing," Warren wrote.

title: Mortgage Rates Spike to New 15-Month High of 6.76% as Bond Market Implodes
author: Snejana Farberov
preview: The average rate on 30-year fixed mortgages increased to 6.76% for the week ending Sept. 10, up 5 basis points from last week.
summary_raw: The average rate on 30-year fixed mortgages increased to 6.76% for the week ending Sept. 10, up 5 basis points from last week.
content_encoded_raw:
Mortgage rates climbed to a 15-month high this week, moving in tandem with surging Treasury yields driven upward by spiking inflation expectations.

The average rate on 30-year fixed home loans jumped to 6.76% for the week ending Sept. 10, up 5 basis points from 6.71% the previous week and the highest since late June 2025, according to Freddie Mac. For perspective, rates averaged 6.35% one year ago.

"The 30-year fixed-rate mortgage averaged 6.76% this week," says Sam Khater, Freddie Mac's chief economist. "Aspiring buyers should remember shopping around for the best mortgage rate and getting multiple quotes can potentially save them thousands."

The 10-year Treasury yields, which mortgage rates closely track, topped 4.9% on Thursday, marking the highest level since November 2023. This was in response to oil prices exceeding $100 a barrel, driven by the U.S.-Iran conflict unfolding with no resolution in sight.  

"Each round of renewed tensions has reinforced the same dynamic that has driven rates higher since late February: oil prices rise, inflation fears follow, and bond markets reprice accordingly," says Realtor.com® senior economist Anthony Smith. 

August's jobs report came in above consensus expectations, with payrolls increasing 162,000 and prior months revised upward, but the strong print barely moved the odds of a rate hike at the upcoming September meeting of the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC).

"The Fed's attention, and the bond market's, is almost entirely on inflation right now, not the labor market," stresses Smith. 

That puts Friday’s consumer price index (CPI) release in the spotlight as the decisive indicator ahead of the FOMC summit. 

"A hotter-than-expected reading would strengthen the case for a hike and add further pressure on mortgage rates," says Smith. “A cooler one could offer some relief.”

Financial markets now put the probability of the Fed raising rates next week at 69.8%, according to CME FedWatch.

On the housing front, August data showed pending sales growth turned negative for the first time since last November. 

“Pricing and delisting trends, while slightly more encouraging, haven't been enough to offset the drag from elevated rates,” points out Smith. “The market that could have been, with rates below 6% and spring momentum building, feels increasingly distant.” 

The economist forecasts that until there is meaningful relief on inflation or a durable resolution to the conflict in Iran, that housing outlook is unlikely to change.

How your credit score affects your mortgage

Your credit score plays a role when you apply for a mortgage. A credit score will determine whether you qualify for a mortgage and the interest rate you'll receive. The higher the credit score, the lower the interest rate you'll qualify for.

The credit score you need will vary depending on the type of loan. A score of 620 is a "fair" rating. However, people applying for a Federal Housing Administration loan might be able to get approved with a credit score of 500, which is considered a low score.

Homebuyers with credit scores of 740 or higher are typically considered to be in very good standing and can usually qualify for better rates, which can reduce monthly payments.

Different types of mortgage loan programs have their own minimum credit score requirements. Some lenders have stricter criteria when evaluating whether to approve a loan. Ultimately, they want to make sure you're able to pay back the loan.

title: Kris Jenner’s Security Intercepts Suspected Stalker Following Alleged Attempt To Reach Her L.A. Home
author: Kelsi Karruli
preview: Zenwilliam Robson, 25, was detained by Jenner's security before he could reach her home, which is situated in the Santa Monica Mountains.
summary_raw: Zenwilliam Robson, 25, was detained by Jenner's security before he could reach her home, which is situated in the Santa Monica Mountains.
content_encoded_raw:
A man suspected of stalking Kris Jenner was arrested in the neighborhood of her Los Angeles home—after trying to contact her multiple times.

Zenwilliam Robson, 25, was detained by Jenner's security before he could reach her home, which is situated in the Santa Monica Mountains, sources told TMZ.

Jenner's security made it clear to authorities that Robson had attempted to contact the "Keeping Up with the Kardashians" star, 70, several times before strolling around her neighborhood.

The Los Angeles County Sheriff's Department arrested the 25-year-old on suspicion of stalking. He was then charged with one misdemeanor count of trespassing and refusing to leave private property.

It is unclear if Jenner was home at the time of the incident.

In addition to her famous "Keeping Up with the Kardashians" property, Jenner also owns two homes in Hidden Hills.

She picked up one abode in 2017 for just under $10 million but sold that off just three years later, having renovated the home extensively before deciding to put it back on the market.

That property was located across the street from her daughter Kim's house.

In 2020, the mother and daughter duo were understood to have bought adjacent abodes in the exclusive neighborhood, with Kris paying $20 million for her piece of the property pie.

Eager to ensure that her latest home buy could serve as her longterm residence, Kris embarked on a gut renovation of the existing structure to create her dream abode, which she unveiled to the world in a 2022 episode of "The Kardashians."

And it appears that plan worked, given that she's now finally walking away from the residence that has served as something of a "backup" abode for so many years.

Though it may no longer be to Kris' tastes, the home in question offers an array of top-of-the-line amenities and decor features, starting with the oh-so-iconic entryway, which the listing describes as a "soaring foyer."

"From the moment you enter, you're greeted by a breathtaking double staircase in a soaring foyer, setting the tone for the grandeur within," the description states.

The primary suite offers an enormous spa-inspired bathroom, as well as a fireplace, wet bar, steam shower, and gym, with the listing describing it as a "private retreat."

"With endless opportunities for relaxation and recreation, this home is truly one-of-a-kind," the listing concludes. "Live like a star in this legendary estate where timeless elegance meets Hollywood prestige."

Jenner has been attempting to sell the family's iconic Los Angeles mansion since February 2025, having used the residence as her family's primary dwelling for more than a decade, throughout which it featured prominently in the Kardashians' popular E! reality series.

"Keeping Up With the Kardashians" fans will immediately recognize the six-bedroom property's dramatic black-and-white entryway, which features two grand staircases that lead up to the second floor.

Jenner, who is mother to Kim, Kourtney, Khloe, Kendall, Kylie, and Rob, purchased the home with her former spouse, Caitlyn Jenner, for $4 million in 2010—three years after the Kardashians' wildly popular series debuted.

However, in the 15 years since she bought the home, Kris' life has changed dramatically—as have the lives of her children.

In 2015, she and her spouse divorced after more than 20 years of marriage and just a few months later, Caitlyn came out as transgender during an interview with ABC News' Diane Sawyer.

Kris, who is now in a relationship with talent manager Corey Gamble, has also expanded her property portfolio and no longer uses the enormous abode as her primary residence.

Her children have also welcomed kids of their own and purchased their own sprawling megamansions in and around Los Angeles—and beyond.

Speaking about her initial decision to sell the expansive 8,000-square-foot abode, Kris told The New York Times that she believes the time has come for another family to make their own memories within its walls.

"I’ve shared so many unforgettable memories in this incredible home with my family, and I’m excited to see it start a new chapter with its next owners," she said.

The outlet noted that nobody is living in the property—which is listed with Tomer Fridman of Christie's International Real Estate Southern California—and the furniture featured in the listing photos was brought in especially to fill the home while it is on the market.

title: Chris Rock Has ‘Complicated’ Feelings About His New Los Angeles Home as a Native New Yorker
author: Hannah Chambers
preview: The comedian recently acquired an L.A. property but finds the city "weird" despite the great weather.
summary_raw: The comedian recently acquired an L.A. property but finds the city "weird" despite the great weather.
content_encoded_raw:
Chris Rock recently acquired a new home in Los Angeles, and the New York City-raised comedian already seems to have a “complicated” relationship with the locale.

“It’s weird,” the 61-year-old star said while speaking with Variety to promote his latest directorial project, “Misty Green," which he explained is a film about a fictional actress, but also about the city of L.A.

"L.A. has got very wonky priorities," Rock said. "There's a real estate office on the same street as The Ivy on Robertson, and in the window, there are houses for $30-$40 million. But there's a homeless guy sleeping right outside. The movie is about that crazy dichotomy."

While Rock has spent plenty of time in Los Angeles with his Hollywood ties, he's recently become much better acquainted with the city.

“I just bought a place there, so I winter in L.A.,” he said. “I love parts of it.”

Rock went on to question some of the things he’s observed since acquiring his new abode, primarily associated with fame and the film industry.

“The average movie studio, like Paramount, what’s in Paramount?” he asked hypothetically. “There’s cameras, sound equipment. But what are you gonna do with that? Can you really steal that stuff?”

“There’s more value at the average Home Depot than at Paramount, but Paramount’s got armed guards,” he continued. “Why? Because they have dreams in there. And people will do anything to get to their dreams.”

Rock noted that throughout his decades-long career—in which he gained prominence as a member of “Saturday Night Live” in the early 1990s—he’s seen a “switch” regarding the concept of fame.

“It used to be that everybody wanted to be great—a great singer, great actor, great comedian,” he said. “Now it’s just game, and the greatness is almost assumed. I mean, you’re always gonna be outed at some point if you don’t have the goods. But L.A. is the mecca of that.”

“It can be beautiful. It’s got the best weather in the world,” Rock admitted. “But it also attracts an underbelly that people want to pretend doesn’t exist.”

The comic then offered his own philosophy on wealth management, and his decision to keep expenses modest despite his success. These themes are tackled in "Misty Green," as the characters are pressured to take on work they're less-than inspired by in order to maintain a lavish lifestyle.

"I've been lucky. I've made some money. I'm not swimming in it. I'm not on jets all the time. I don't own a boat," Rock explained. "How much are your monthly bills? Because if you can keep your monthly low enough, you can say no to things. I don't own a car."

"Yeah, I have a place in New York and L.A., but I don't even have a doorman," he continued. "I live on a normal block in both places. You can ring by bell. It doesn't say 'Rock' on the bell, but you can ring my bell. And I do this purposely, so I don't have to do things I don't want to do."

Although Rock may be keeping things affordable by Hollywood standards, he has spent decades living in the affluent neighborhood of Alpine, NJ—a mainstay on most-expensive-ZIP-code lists over time.

"Showbiz has been very, very good to me. In a world where we have trillionaires, I don't have that much money," he said.

The comic turned director purchased the 10,300-square-foot, Colonial-style home in 2001. It sits on more than 2 acres.

He’s made a handful of public comments about his Garden State home over the years, dedicating a bit in his 2008 special, “Kill the Messenger” to the town.

While Alpine is much more under the radar than L.A., it’s still home to plenty of celebrities.

In 2024, New Jersey Monthly dubbed it the “Beverly Hills” of the state, noting the ultraprivate neighborhood just 15 miles outside of Manhattan has attracted the likes of Stevie Wonder, Britney Spears, Mary J. Blige, and fellow “Saturday Night Live” former cast member, Tracy Morgan.

Perhaps the title was inspired by a comment Rock made in 2014, during an interview with Vulture, in which he said, “I’m in Alpine. That’s not Jersey. That’s like Beverly Hills with freaking snow.”

Rock seems to have a habit of holding onto real estate for the long haul.

In 2022, he offloaded his former Brooklyn apartment for $3.25 million. He had originally purchased the home in 1994, but moved out shortly after marrying his now ex-wife, Malaak Compton-Rock, in 1996.

The 3,7000-square-foot Clinton Hill carriage house was not your average pad. Built in 1899, the historical home boasted exposed ceiling beams and sturdy brick walls, and even included a two-car garage. For the nearly two decades he held onto it before selling, Rock offered the apartment as a rental, priced anywhere from $7,950 to $15,000.

Following his 2016 divorce from Compton-Rock, the comedian and his family continued to live in Alpine. The couple share two daughters—Lola Simone Rock, 24, and Zahra Savannah Rock, 22. According to the New York Post, he purchased another home in the neighborhood post-split, likely to stay close to his children.

"Chris is still on very good terms with Malaak," a source told The Post. "He loves his daughters and spends a lot of time with them."

title: Home Sales Plunge to 14-Month Low as Rising Mortgage Rates Stun Buyers
author: Snejana Farberov
preview: Existing-home sales fell 2% month over month and 1.2% to a seasonally adjusted annual rate of 3.98 million, the lowest since June 2025.
summary_raw: Existing-home sales fell 2% month over month and 1.2% to a seasonally adjusted annual rate of 3.98 million, the lowest since June 2025.
content_encoded_raw:
Home selling suffered a setback in August, both on a monthly and annual basis, as surging mortgage rates kept more would-be buyers on the sidelines at the end of summer.

Existing-home sales decreased to a seasonally adjusted annual rate of 3.98 million, down 2% from July and 1.2% from a year ago, the National Association of Realtors® reported Thursday. The last time sales dipped below the 4 million threshold was in June 2025.

Falling behind the year-ago pace, the August sales snapped a four-month streak of annual gains.

"Mortgage rates and home sales move in opposite directions, so it's not surprising to see a mild dip in home buying activity due to high mortgage rates," says NAR Chief Economist Lawrence Yun.

The 30-year fixed-rate mortgage climbed to 6.71% on Sept. 3, its highest level in more than a year, according to Freddie Mac, as renewed inflation fears triggered a large-scale bond sell-off.

"With a rate hike in play at next week’s Fed meeting, higher mortgage rates are likely in the near-term, which will keep homebuying costs high, but the expectation of higher financing costs on the horizon could encourage buyers to move ahead rather than wait, creating mixed pressures for buyers this fall," says Realtor.com® chief economist Danielle Hale.

At the same time, existing home sales are actually up 1.6% year to date through the first eight months of the year.  

"That is showing some stability in home sales ... but also the fact that the resiliency of homebuyers is still not falling apart," says Yun on a call with reporters.

At the regional level, month-over-month sales held steady in the West but slumped in the Northeast, Midwest and South. Meanwhile, annual sales declined everywhere except the South, where they remained flat.

Yun points out that despite the persistently high borrowing costs cooling sales, homebuying demand is being propped up by rising wages, which increased 3.2% in August, according to the latest better-than-expected jobs report.

"Job creation and wage growth typically drive housing demand," points out the economist.

Even as sales contracted, the median sales price continued rising, edging up 1.6% year over year to $429,100, a record high for the month of August. This marks the 38th consecutive month of annual price gains.

Reflecting regional variation, the Northeast led the nation in annual price gain, which surged 4.3%, to $556,900. The Midwest saw the second-biggest growth of 3.3% from August 2025, to $340,400.

In the well-supplied South, prices ticked up 0.7% year over year, reaching $366,500, while the West experienced an annual downturn of 0.2%, coming in at $619,100.

Single-family home sales fell 1.9% from July to a seasonally adjusted rate of 3.62 million properties, down 1.1% compared to a year ago. Meanwhile, condominium and co-op sales dropped 2.7% both month over month and year over year to 360,000 units.

Growing inventory

Looking at the national housing supply, total inventory in August hit 1.62 million units, up 3.2% from July and up 5.9% from year-ago levels. This is the first time since November 2019 that inventory exceeded 1.6 million units.

At the same time, the number of months it would take to exhaust the nation's unsold inventory reached 4.9 months' supply, the highest level in over a decade.

"The ample supply of homes for sale on the market is giving homebuyers better opportunities to negotiate," says Yun.

According to Hale, that means homebuyers saw the best market-balance conditions on average nationwide in more than a decade.

In more good news, housing affordability improved in every part of the U.S., with the West leading the pack (5.9%), followed by the south (4.5%), the Midwest (1.7%), and the Northeast (0.5%).

Mixed indicators

Realtor.com data shows that new listings remained sluggish in both July and August, not topping their prior year pace as was common in the spring, but active listings continued to climb. 

"Home sellers have largely sidestepped disappointment this summer and are sticking with the market rather than delisting, a marked contrast to 2025, but relatively flat new listings signal caution among potential sellers," notes Hale. "This caution will likely keep slowing home sales from tipping the market abruptly in favor of buyers."

On top of that, the share of first-time home buyers rose to 30%, up from both the prior month and prior year.

"As mortgage rates climb, the lock-in for existing homeowners with low outstanding mortgage rates grows," says Hale. "A stronger lock-in may mean we see an increased share of first-time homebuyers in the months ahead, which also tend to rank among the friendliest for homebuyers seasonally."

title: Hoda Kotb Reunites With Ex-Fiancé Joel Schiffman at Her $2.9 Million New York Home for Daughters’ Major Milestone
author: Kelsi Karruli
preview: The former host took to Instagram to document the occasion as Haley and Hope headed back to the classroom for fourth and second grade.
summary_raw: The former host took to Instagram to document the occasion as Haley and Hope headed back to the classroom for fourth and second grade.
content_encoded_raw:
Hoda Kotb and her ex-fiance, Joel Schiffman, reunited at her $2.9 million Bronxville, NY, home to celebrate a major milestone for their two daughters, Haley and Hope: the first day of school.

The former "Today" show host, 62, took to Instagram to document the special occasion as Haley, 9, and Hope, 7, headed back to the classroom for fourth and second grade, respectively.

Before sending the girls off to school, Kotb posed outside her suburban New York home alongside Schiffman, 68, and their daughters, with the foursome smiling together for a sweet family photo.

Another image captured the family of four walking down the street, hand in hand as they marked the start of the new school year.

“It’s here! First day of school. 4th and 2nd grade! Whaaaatttt?” Kotb wrote alongside the images.

The milestone comes nearly two years after Kotb announced in September 2024 that she would be stepping away from "Today," explaining that she wanted to spend more time with her children.

And this isn't the first time Schiffman has joined Kotb and their daughters at her suburban home since the former couple ended their engagement in 2022.

He previously showed up to her NY home for a heartwarming Father's Day celebration.

Kotb, who ended her eight-year relationship with Schiffman in 2022, paid tribute to her former partner in the caption, writing, "Best Father's Day to the best father."

He also previously took a trip to the upstate New York home for a "funday Sunday."

The former couple also spent Father's Day together last year at Kotb's $2.9 million home, which she purchased in April 2024, shortly before she quit the "Today" show.

Although Schiffman and Kotb once lived together in New York City with their kids, the mother of two made the decision in 2024 to move her children to the suburbs in a bid to give them more "normality," while it's thought her former partner remained in Manhattan.

However, he made sure to take a break from the honking taxis and towering skyscrapers to make a trip to Bronxville, which is a mere 30-minute drive from Manhattan.

Kotb previously revealed that her move from the city had also been motivated, at least in part, by her daughter Hope's Type 1 diabetes diagnosis.

"As anyone with a child who has Type 1 [diabetes], especially a little kid, you're constantly watching, you're constantly monitoring, you're constantly checking, which is what I did all the time when I was [on the 'Today' show]. You’re distracted," she shared on a May 28 appearance on Today.

"You just get a priority check in your life. I can be here and sweating what’s happening to Hope in the morning and in the night, or I can be there and feel relief that I can see."

Kotb first revealed that her younger daughter was struggling with a health issue in March 2023, when she explained that Hope had been hospitalized for an undisclosed condition.

Less than two years later, Kotb decided to move her family to Bronxville, where she purchased a stunning property just a short walk from her kids' school.

Speaking to Today.com ahead of her last day on the show, Kotb opened up about her desire to embrace a new routine with her kids at the four-bedroom, five-bathroom, center-hall Colonial.

She was excited to have a more "normal" day-to-day regimen after years of early mornings, she explained.

"I'm just going to let us be a family with a normal rhythm of life. See what we become," the on-air celebrity, who was replaced by Craig Melvin, said.

"I'm going to let [my daughters] take more trips and stay up a little later because part of the reason I put them to bed at that hour is because I've got to go to bed. I'm like, 'Goodnight! Everyone's going to bed.' They're like, 'It's 6:30!' I'm like, 'Yeah, lights out!'"

Kotb said in August that she had a vision when it came to finding the perfect family home, revealing in an episode of “Today” that she wanted to create a “warm and cozy” environment where her children could relax and find sanctuary.

“It’s all new,” she said of her move. “New kids, new school, new things, new everything. And it’s funny because all I could think of was that I wanted my house for the kids to feel warm and cozy and a place where they want to hang. And that’s it.”

She previously gave fans a rare glimpse at the cozy workout center inside her upstate New York home during a sweet video with her daughter.

Kotb briefly returned to the "Today" show to fill in for Savannah Guthrie who took a leave of absence after her mother, Nancy Guthrie, was abducted from her Arizona home.

title: See What Your Housing Budget Buys in Every ZIP Code
author: Keith Griffith
preview: A new tool from Realtor.com breaks down what share of homes located in each ZIP code would be affordable at your price point.
summary_raw: A new tool from Realtor.com breaks down what share of homes located in each ZIP code would be affordable at your price point.
content_encoded_raw:
For homebuyers, setting a realistic budget is a smart step early in the process. Once that's done, narrowing down a neighborhood for your home search gets easier.

A new tool from the Realtor.com® economic research team breaks down what share of homes located in each ZIP code would be attainable based on a buyer's budget.

To roughly estimate your affordable price range for a home, a common rule of thumb recommends targeting a home that is no more than three to five times your annual income—unless you are bringing significant cash to the table from a prior home sale.

Using that guideline, a family making the median household income of $83,700 could afford a home that's priced from around $250,000 on the conservative end, to $418,000 on the most aggressive side. The exact budget would depend on a buyer's down payment, existing debt, and mortgage rates.

Nationally, 28% of existing homes would be affordable to buyers with a budget of $250,000, and 58% would be within reach of buyers who are able to spend $418,000, according to the new Realtor.com analysis.

However, home values vary greatly across the country, and a buyer with a $250,000 budget will find many more options within their price range in Ohio than California, for example.

Even within the same metro area, prices can vary depending on the neighborhood. That’s where the new ZIP code affordability mapping tool can help prospective buyers target their search based on their budget.

To determine how far a specific budget will go in each ZIP code, we’ve analyzed the estimated property values of more than 100 million homes across the nation to see how many of them fall within a range of price points from $100,000 (3% of listings nationally) to $10 million (99.9% of listings). 

For example, in New York City, the typical home costs around $800,000. But in the ZIP code covering Battery Park City, just 1% of all homes would be affordable at that price.

Meanwhile, in certain parts of Staten Island and the Bronx, nearly every home could be purchased on a budget of $800,000.

The most exclusive ZIP codes

In every ZIP code with at least 50 identifiable homes for valuation analysis, a $10 million budget should be able to afford at least half of the homes in the area. 

The least affordable ZIP code in the nation is 94027 in Atherton, CA, where a $10 million budget could afford just 59% of the homes.

An exclusive bedroom community in Silicon Valley, Atherton is home to NBA star Steph Curry, Google co-founder Eric Schmidt, and venture capitalist Marc Andreessen, among other tech luminaries.

The second most expensive ZIP code is 33109 in Miami Beach, FL. That ZIP code is exclusive to Fisher Island, an ultraexclusive enclave where notables such as Oprah Winfrey, Julia Roberts, and Andre Agassi have owned homes.

In Aspen, CO, ZIP code 81612 is the third most exclusive housing market in the nation, where a budget of $10 million can afford just 70% of the available properties.

Known globally as an exclusive ski resort, Aspen is the playground of the ultrarich, and properties there can run into the hundreds of millions.

Other ZIP codes on the most exclusive list include Sagaponack, NY; Newport Coast, CA; and Woody Creek, CO.

The most affordable ZIP codes

Across the nation, our analysis identified only two ZIP codes where there are at least 50 homes, and a homebuying budget of $100,000 is enough to afford every single home in the area.
