Those ZIP codes are located in Elbert and Squire, both tiny communities in the remote, rugged mountains of southern West Virginia.

Formerly sustained by coal mining, this region has fallen on hard times, and economic opportunities are limited due to the inaccessible terrain and sparse population.

In total, seven of the 10 most affordable ZIP codes in the nation are located in West Virginia, underscoring the state's relatively cheap housing stock in comparison to the rest of the country.

The other ZIP codes are located in East St. Louis, IL, and Flint, MI, both hardscrabble cities facing significant economic challenges.

Like other cities that appear on this list, East St. Louis has suffered significant population decline in recent decades, leading to a surplus of homes, many of which are left in disrepair.

Although it was once a busy industrial town on the Mississippi River, East St. Louis suffered significant job losses due to globalization as manufacturing jobs moved overseas.

The city’s population of about 18,000 is down more than two-thirds from where it stood in 1980.

In Austin, TX, data mapping shows a stark divide in buying opportunities on a $500,000 budget.

title: Inside Retired MLB Star David Eckstein and Actress Ashley Eckstein’s Fantasy Florida Home
author: Karli Mullane
preview: The retired MLB star, 51, and his wife, 44, bought the five-bedroom, five-bathroom Orlando, FL, home in 2020.
summary_raw: The retired MLB star, 51, and his wife, 44, bought the five-bedroom, five-bathroom Orlando, FL, home in 2020.
content_encoded_raw:
The story behind retired MLB player David Eckstein meeting his wife, Disney actress Ashley Eckstein, is nothing short of a fairy tale—so it's fitting that they're living out their happily ever after in a Florida home base that meets all their design needs.

David, 51, and Ashley, 44, bought the five-bedroom, five-bathroom, 4,200-square-foot Orlando, FL, residence in 2020, the same year it was built. Since then, they've adorned the interior of the English cottage-style home in a way that marries their passion for the ballpark and their favorite Disney theme park, Walt Disney World.

David, a two-time World Series Champion and MVP of the 2006 World Series when he played for the St. Louis Cardinals, and Ashley, the voice of Ahsoka Tano in all seven seasons of the “Star Wars: The Clone Wars” series, are both Orlando locals who grew up going to the Magic Kingdom, and now consider it “almost a requirement” to live close by.

“When you grow up in Orlando, Disney is a part of you,” David reveals to Realtor.com in the latest Celebrity Sanctuary. “It was always something that was really special because we didn't have much money and my mom would save up to take us once a year, if not every three years, and it was the most magical place on Earth.”

“It's all I can remember,” adds Ashley, whose father was a Disney cast member and whose mother was a school teacher who treated the park like a classroom. “I say I was raised by Disney because we were at Walt Disney World at least once a week—Disney is in my DNA, and so that was one thing we bonded over instantly.”

The couple discovered their shared affinity for all things Disney. Both have written books that recount the introduction from different perspectives.

“Just Enough” is David's memoir of his life and storied sports career, while “Lucky 22” is Ashley's debut romance novel she co-wrote with romance author Samantha Chase. The latter is a fictionalized narrative about the start of the couple's relationship.

“How we met and fell in love is a chapter in David's book and that's all it deserves to be ... but I had a feeling that people were going to want to know more because it’s a very serendipitous story,” shares Ashley. She notes that her romanticized written version is “actually about 90% true.”

The fortuitous chain of events began when Ashley attended a baseball game wearing the jersey number David had been randomly assigned because it happened to be the favorite numeral of the Her Universe founder.

“My boyfriend at the time gave me David's shirt because that was my favorite number, and so the whole game, I was watching ‘my boy,’” she explains. “I just happened to be looking at the dugout because one of the players scored—there was a bunch of commotion, and since I was in the front row, he happened to look over and we locked eyes.” 

Both books, which dropped on Sept. 8, cover this special chapter in the Ecksteins’ lives that eventually led to their tying the knot in 2005 and making several house moves together.

In this installment of Celebrity Sanctuary, the authors detail the novel Disney and baseball-inspired decor at their O-Town domain, particularly the ones reserved for their complementary mudroom and media room sanctuary spaces that they’ve designed to be in a league of their own.

Ashley: What motivated our move back to Orlando was the fact that it is home for both of us. We like to say home is wherever your family is. Luckily for us, our families live in Orlando and we both love Disney, so it works out for us.

What motivated our move to our house now is the fact that it's very close to Disney. Literally minutes. We've also lived in California and we lived very close to Disneyland, so it's just kind of a life rule.

I do a lot of work with Disney, and the proximity to the parks works well for me because it's close to my office, as you could say.

The overall interior aesthetic is Disney. When David played baseball, we were always moving. In fact, one year we moved nine times in one year, so we were always living out of a suitcase.

Once David retired, we were able to finally settle down. When we moved into this home in 2020, David told me, “I want this to be our forever home and you can decorate it however you want.” 

I said, “Really, however I want?” And he said, “Yes. Just give me a TV wall with several TVs” so he can watch multiple games at once. So I decided to decorate the entire house inspired by "Alice in Wonderland" with a little bit of "Cinderella" and a corner for David.

David: It's the mudroom. She gave me a little corner. When you walk into the corner, the way they had constructed it, it actually looked like three lockers and so we made it into three lockers. 

I played for the University of Florida, so we have one locker with the Gators. We have one locker with the Angels, and we have one locker with the Cardinals. We decorated it off of Disney's [baseball-themed restaurant], Casey's Corner, and so we have the big circular emblem of David's Corner. 

Ashley: We replicated one of the signs of Casey's Corner, but made it David's Corner. I worked with a friend [whose] job for Disney is to build themed spaces. 

I'm also best friends with the official voice of Mickey Mouse for Disney. His name is Brett Iwin, and he's a Disney fine artist. He's an incredible artist, and he helped us build the space. 

I have a vision and I can tell the story in my mind, but I am not an artist. So I work with my friends to say, “Here's what I want. Help me bring it to life.”

Now, the joke is that I only gave him a corner. However, in fairness, David didn't want to showcase any of his baseball memorabilia. It was really sad; we had these World Series-worn jerseys and cleats and all this incredible memorabilia just sitting in bins. 

When we bought the house, the mudroom was already built and it already looked like a baseball locker room. I told David, “I don't care if you don't want it, this is meant to be a baseball locker room.” 

I had a vision of Casey's Corner, but making it David's Corner, and I said, “We’re giving you a baseball area.”

He jokes about it now, but if it were up to him, there wouldn't be any baseball in the house. I love my husband. He is very humble, but I am a proud wife, so I like to show off what he's accomplished.

David: When we first met, she came over to my apartment and my World Series-winning uniform was on the floor in my closet. When you read my book, you'll understand that I never thought I was good enough. For me to actually go, “Oh, my gosh, I did something great,” was not in me. Then Ashley's here, like, “No, you need to display this.” 

Don't get me wrong, I'm going to tell you right now, I have gotten a lot of joy in that room now. Being able to walk by, seeing all the stuff, my World Series jerseys, from University of Florida to the Angels to the Gators to the Cardinals, all right there. The game-winning bat that I won World Series MVP with is in there. Some of the awards that I had won. How they created the room, it's actually really, really nice.

What sanctuary is to me, it's where I can relax with peace and quiet and just enjoy. I know we're [talking] about my corner, but I would have to say [my sanctuary is] actually on the couch in front of my three TVs, having the ability to watch multiple games at the same time. That's what I've always loved, and that was my one request of the home, was that I had the ability to sit on a couch that reclines and watch games.

Ashley: We're very happy with our home and our space, but Walt Disney had a quote, I don't have it memorized, but he's basically saying that the Disney parks are always in motion. They're never finished. That's the way we look at our home. David's Corner is always evolving. He actually has all of his first-hit baseballs—grand slam baseball, first home run for every team and for the big leagues—and so we want to hang up all those baseballs.

David: Baseball cards and maybe wallpaper. 

Ashley: That's the next phase for David's Corner. 

What I say about the house is it brings us joy. I've never followed any rules when it comes to interior design. In fact, I feel like I’ve broken every interior design rule, and I don’t care because your home is where you spend half your life if not more, and it should bring you joy. 

When we walk in our home, it literally makes me smile. I walk past all my "Alice in Wonderland" things or even David’s Corner, and it brings the biggest smile to my face in the midst of daily stresses. The fact that we’ve built a home that brings us joy, we hope that others will do the same.

title: Massachusetts Requires Data Centers To Get Local Approvals in Latest Clampdown
author: Tristan Navera
preview: Data center developers must now secure a community benefits agreement, which outlines how they'll benefit the areas where they operate.
summary_raw: Data center developers must now secure a community benefits agreement, which  outlines how they'll benefit the areas where they operate.
content_encoded_raw:
Massachusetts Gov. Maura Healey has signed an executive order to prevent data centers from seeking state-level approvals without local support.

Healey's new order prevents data centers over 25 megawatts from seeking state permits unless they have local approvals. She also directed the state's agencies to enforce a framework she announced this summer requiring the developments to have a clean energy supply, water resources, and community feedback before advancing.

It's the latest effort as lawmakers try to rein in the fast-growing data center industry nationwide. Thousands of new data center proposals have brought impacts on the housing market and energy prices. They've also emerged as a midterms flashpoint, as political parties try to contend with how to regulate the industry.

“Unless a community says yes to a data center, we are saying no,” Healey said in a statement. “We’re giving communities a voice and laying out the rules for what needs to happen in Massachusetts."

A poll from NBC News released this week found 69% of respondents oppose the construction of data centers in their local area. Democrats and independents are notably more opposed than Republicans.

The governor also prohibited nondisclosure agreements between state agencies and data center developers, in favor of transparency.

Tech investor Kevin Xu tracked three active moratoria on data center development in Massachusetts, including Lowell, Westfield, and Holyoke. Four other areas are considering them.

Data center debate

Specifically, data centers must now secure a community benefits agreement, a type of plan created for large energy projects. These outline how the developer will engage with local communities while they build and operate the data centers.

They also require a negotiated agreement that lays out anticipated impacts on that locality and what benefits its gains from the project. Only when one is in place will the state begin reviewing permits.

But the state wants only to add guardrails to the data center developments, not halt them entirely, Healey said.

Chrissy Lynch, president of the Massachusetts AFL-CIO, said in a statement that data center construction in the nation supports tens of thousands of union jobs.

"We need rules to ensure that these data centers support union jobs for local people, that they provide their own water and energy, that they pay their fair share of taxes, and that they work with local communities to ensure that the economic benefits are truly felt by those communities," Lynch said.

Republican Mike Minogue, who is challenging Healey for governorship this fall, criticized her prior stance. The state previously had a data center sales tax exemption that allowed data center operators to buy servers and other equipment. But Healey paused that exemption for new projects in June.

"Maura Healey rolled out the red carpet for data centers," Minogue said in a Facebook post. "They got tax breaks on the backs of hard-working Massachusetts families. Now she wants to re-write history because she's up for re-election."

title: Former Fed Chair Jerome Powell Sells Gibson Island Mansion for $7.2 Million
author: Snejana Farberov
preview: Jerome Powell sold his exclusive waterfront retreat in an off-market transaction just months after finishing his term as Fed chair.
summary_raw: Jerome Powell sold his exclusive waterfront retreat in an off-market transaction just months after finishing his term as Fed chair.
content_encoded_raw:
Less than three months after concluding his term as Federal Reserve chair, Jerome Powell sold his sprawling waterfront mansion on Maryland's ultraexclusive Gibson Island for $7.2 million.

Public property records reviewed by Realtor.com® indicate that the six-bedroom, eight-bathroom, 7,155-square-foot property sitting on a 2-acre lot exchanged hands on Aug. 4.

Powell's luxury retreat was not listed on a multiple listing service, and the sale was off-market, as Baltimore Business Journal first reported on Wednesday.  

Realtor.com® reached out to listing agent Sarah Kanne at Gibson Island Real Estate seeking comment on the sale, but has not received an immediate response.

Located just an hour from Washington, DC, the 2004-built shingle-style mansion sits in a private enclave off the coast of Maryland. Described in listing materials as an "exquisite waterfront residence," Powell's former vacation home offers water views from nearly every principal room.

The listing notes that the property combing coastal architecture and superior craftsmanship "has been meticulously maintained by its current owners."

The estate facing the Magothy River also features a waterfront swimming pool, a private pier with a boat lift, stone terraces, and manicured lawns.  

Powell purchased the home for $3.86 million in 2006, around the time when he co-founded Severn Capital Partners, a private equity firm. 

A year later, he joined the members-only Gibson Island Club, according to disclosure records produced by the Senate Banking, Housing and Urban Affairs Committee in 2017 in relation to his Federal Reserve nomination.

Real estate holdings

Powell and his wife, film producer Elissa Leonard, also own a neighboring home on Gibson Island, which they picked up for $3 million, according to the records.

Gibson Island is one of the most exclusive ZIP codes in Maryland, with a year-round population of fewer than 230 inhabitants.

The power couple's portfolio is anchored by their primary residence in Chevy Chase, MD, purchased in 2006 for $3 million.

Built in 1903, the elegant two-story home comes with a pool and a two-car garage. It is located on a tree-lined street.

Powell, 73, concluded his eight-year tenure at the helm of the Fed in May of this year and was succeeded by Kevin Warsh. However, he remains on the Federal Reserve Board of Governors.

During his time as chair, Powell was frequently criticized by President Donald Trump for failing to drastically reduce interest rates. 

In January, the Department of Justice opened a criminal investigation into Powell over his congressional testimony concerning the cost of renovations to the Federal Reserve headquarters. The probe was dropped in April without any charges being filed.

title: Jimmy Kimmel’s Late-Night Reign Is Reportedly Coming to an End—Inside the Lavish California Home Where He Could Retreat
author: Kelsi Karruli
preview: Kimmel's career has made plenty of headlines over the past year, and now the comedian is reportedly preparing to leave the show behind.
summary_raw: Kimmel's career has made plenty of headlines over the past year, and now the comedian is reportedly preparing to leave the show behind.
content_encoded_raw:
TV host Jimmy Kimmel may soon mark the end of his decades-long run in late-night TV—leaving fans with one big question: Where will he retreat once the cameras stop rolling?

Kimmel's on-air career has made plenty of headlines over the past year, and now the comedian is reportedly preparing to leave "Jimmy Kimmel Live!" when his current contract comes to an end.

“His contract is not getting extended,” a source told the outlet.

That would bring the show to an end in May 2027, more than 24 years after Kimmel first took his seat behind the late-night desk.

However, those reports have been disputed by ABC.

“This information is inaccurate—any reports about the future of the show at this point are purely speculative," a spokesperson for ABC Entertainment told The Hill.

The potential conclusion of Kimmel's tenure comes after a particularly turbulent period for the host.

In September 2025, Kimmel made an emotional return to his popular show just days after he was suspended "indefinitely" by ABC over controversial statements he made in the aftermath of the murder of conservative activist Charlie Kirk.

At the time, Kimmel was overcome with emotion as he took to the stage in front of a live audience at his show's Los Angeles studio, receiving a lengthy standing ovation.

The TV host addressed his suspension in his opening monologue, choking back tears as he insisted that he had never meant to "make light of the murder of a young man."

But when Kimmel does step away from the cameras, his real-life sanctuary tells a much quieter story—one rooted in peace, privacy, and distance from the Hollywood spotlight.

Kimmel resides at a sprawling property in Hermosa Beach, CA, where he and his wife, Molly McNearney, the head writer and executive producer of his show, custom-built a residence for their family.

The dwelling sits on two parcels of land that Kimmel snapped up for a combined $8 million in 2017. They total about a half-acre.

Images taken of the property in 2023 revealed that construction was nearing completion, offering a glimpse of the expansive residence and its stunning views over the ocean.

The two-story home also boasts a large swimming pool, creating an idyllic coastal retreat for Kimmel and his family.

When Kimmel purchased the property, the existing residence had four bedrooms and two bathrooms. It has apparently been expanded significantly as part of the custom build.

Kimmel previously owned a home in the Hollywood Hills, which he offloaded in 2014. He is said to own another property near the storied Chateau Marmont hotel, which he reportedly purchased for $1.1 million in 2010.

That same year, Kimmel placed the dwelling in a trust, and it was later reported that he had given use of the home to his sister-in-law, Kelly McNearney.

Yet whenever the comedian steps beyond the walls of his private coastal retreat, he continues to find himself at the center of controversy.

Most recently, President Donald Trump and first lady Melania Trump took to social media to demand that ABC "take a stand" and remove Kimmel from the air following a joke about Melania being an "expectant widow." Kimmel made the joke two days before shots were fired at the White House Correspondents' Dinner.

During the bit, Kimmel portrayed himself as the emcee of the dinner, teasing, "Of course, our first lady, Melania, is here."

He then called her "beautiful" before adding, "Mrs. Trump, you have a glow like an expectant widow.”

The comedian also joked about Donald Trump's age and health.

Kimmel's quips about the Trumps came two days before a gunman broke past a security perimeter and fired shots inside the Washington Hilton on April 25 while the president and first lady were inside.

On April 27, the president took to social media to brand Kimmel's jokes "really shocking" and "something far beyond the pale."

He added, "Jimmy Kimmel should be immediately fired by Disney and ABC."

Mere hours later, Melania added to the discourse.

"His monologue about my family isn’t comedy," she wrote. "His words are corrosive and deepens the political sickness within America.”

The first lady then branded the comedian a "coward" who “shouldn’t have the opportunity to enter our homes each evening to spread hate." She added that he "hides behind ABC because he knows the network will keep running cover to protect him.”

She ended her post with, "Enough is enough. It is time for ABC to take a stand."

White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt also addressed Kimmel's jokes during a briefing.

“This kind of rhetoric about the president, the first lady, and his supporters is completely deranged," Leavitt said. "It’s unbelievable that the American people are consuming it night after night after night.”

Kimmel defended his jokes during his show on the evening of April 27.

"You know how sometimes you wake up in the morning and the first lady puts out a statement demanding you be fired from your job. We’ve all been there, right?” Kimmel said in his opening monologue.

Kimmel said the remark was “obviously a joke about their age difference and the look of joy we see on her face every time they’re together.”

He added, “It was a very light roast joke about the fact that he’s almost 80, and she’s younger than I am. It was not, by any stretch of the definition, a call to assassination, and they know that.”

Kimmel also argued that if Trump believed he should be fired over his comments, the president should consider remarks Leavitt had made just hours before the dinner when she told Fox News, "It will be funny. It will be entertaining. There will be some shots fired tonight.”

The comedian conceded that the incident may have been "stressful" for the president and first lady, but he argued that Melania should discuss dialing back the use of derogatory language with her husband.

“Donald Trump is allowed to say whatever he wants to say, as are you and as am I, as are all of us, because under the First Amendment, we have, as Americans, a right to free speech,” Kimmel said, while insisting that he has been an advocate against gun violence.

“I am sorry that you and the president and everyone in that room on Saturday went through that. I really am," he added. "Just ’cause no one got killed doesn't mean it wasn’t traumatic and scary, and we should come together and be best."

ABC has yet to comment on the remarks made by Kimmel and the Trumps. Realtor.com® has reached out to ABC and Kimmel for comment.

This isn't the first time Kimmel has come under fire for his jokes.

In September 2025, Kimmel was "indefinitely" suspended by ABC after making several controversial statements in the wake of Kirk's murder.

At the time, Kimmel made multiple references to the conservative activist and Turning Point USA founder—who was fatally shot while attending an event at Utah Valley University—and Tyler Robinson, the Utah man accused of killing Kirk.

During his Sept. 15 episode, Kimmel told viewers: "We hit some new lows over the weekend with the MAGA gang desperately trying to characterize this kid who murdered Charlie Kirk as anything other than one of them and doing everything they can to score political points from it.

"In between the finger-pointing, there was grieving."

On Sept. 16, he mentioned Kirk again, this time taking aim at the right.

"Many in MAGA-land are working very hard to capitalize on the murder of Charlie Kirk," he said.

"This is a very, very serious issue right now for Disney. We can do this the easy way or the hard way," he said.

"Disney needs to see some change here, but the individual licensed stations that are taking their content, it's time for them to step up and say this, you know, garbage to the extent that that's what comes down the pipe in the future isn't something that we think serves the needs of our local communities.

"There's calls for Kimmel to be fired. I think you could certainly see a path forward for suspension over this," he said.

Minutes after Carr made those comments, Nexstar Media Group Inc. revealed that it would stop airing the show on its 32 ABC affiliates.

"Mr. Kimmel's comments about the death of Mr. Kirk are offensive and insensitive at a critical time in our national political discourse," Andrew Alford, president of Nexstar's broadcasting division, said.

Shortly after Nexstar announced its decision, ABC, which has FCC-approved licenses for the local broadcast affiliates it owns, issued its own statement about the comedian.

A spokesperson for the Disney-owned network simply said of the decision: "'Jimmy Kimmel Live' will be preempted indefinitely."

Trump praised the decision in a post shared on Truth Social.

"Great News for America: The ratings challenged Jimmy Kimmel Show is CANCELLED. Congratulations to ABC for finally having the courage to do what had to be done,“ Trump wrote.

"Kimmel has ZERO talent, and worse ratings than even [Stephen] Colbert, if that’s possible. That leaves Jimmy and Seth, two total losers, on Fake News NBC. Their ratings are also horrible. Do it NBC!!!”

However, after six days of suspension, Kimmel returned to the stage.

title: Texas Condo Owners Are Still Paying $800 in Monthly HOA Fees 5 Years After Fire Destroyed Units
author: Snejana Farberov
preview: Fire-displaced condo owners remain trapped paying thousands in monthly HOA fees and special assessments on uninhabitable units.
summary_raw: Fire-displaced condo owners remain trapped paying thousands in monthly HOA fees and special assessments on uninhabitable units.
content_encoded_raw:
More than five years after a fast-moving fire destroyed their condominiums, nearly a dozen Texas property owners are still paying hundreds of dollars in monthly HOA fees and special assessments on their uninhabitable units while rebuilding drags on. 

The blaze ignited in March 2021 at Bayfront Towers, a 75-unit complex nestled in the Houston suburb of Nassau Bay, TX. According to ABC13, officials ruled the fire accidental after determining that it originated on a top-floor balcony, yet no specific cause was ever identified.

By the time firefighters extinguished the flames, 11 condos lay in ruins and 26 were left with smoke and water damage requiring remediation. 

Sarah Arends’ first-floor unit, which she purchased three years earlier for her retirement, was among the 11 that were destroyed in the fire. 

Despite being unable to live in her condo, Arends has been paying close to $800 a month in HOA fees to manage and maintain shared community spaces, totaling $10,000 a year. 

Speaking to Fox 26 Houston in August, Arends revealed that she was also hit with $38,000 in special assessments imposed by the board to finance the reconstruction of the ravaged condos. 

Since 2021, Arends, who lives on a fixed income, estimates she has spent $80,000 on a property where she can no longer live while paying out of pocket to rent elsewhere.

In all, Bayfront Condominium Association has raised more than $2.8 million in special assessments after exhausting its insurance payouts to fix up the damaged condos in the first two years after the fire, reported Houston Chronicle.

Stalled rebuilding

Bayfront HOA president Tom Benson, who also lost his condo in the fire, tells Realtor.com® in a statement that it took the board 18 months working through the Harris County Flood District to secure approval to rebuild the units at the existing elevation.

Once that was done, the broad hired an architectural firm to create drawings for the rebuild, but a company buyout delayed the process.

Finally in 2023, the board hired Sunrise Certified Services, a Houston-area contractor, to carry out the reconstruction, which was reportedly slated for completion by May 2026.

"We don't know if it's going to be a month, a year, five years, we don't know," said Arends.

Benson recently told KHOU11 that the contract signed with Sunrise more than three years ago was less than watertight and lacked penalties for missed deadlines. 

"The selected contractor has been a disappointment," the HOA president adds. "Timing to complete is now over a year late. We are working to transition to a new general contractor to finish the job and get owners back in their units before year end."      

Arends offered a blunter assessment of the contractor's work pace.

"I don't know what he's doing; he's just pooping along," she said.

Realtor.com reached out to Sunrise seeking comment but did not receive an immediate response.  

No relief in sight

Fed up with the prolonged wait, Arends has repeatedly called on the board to temporarily exempt the 11 displaced condo owners from paying monthly HOA dues. Her pleas have been rejected because the condo association's bylaws include no emergency fee-relief provisions.

The association is still required to meet all of its ongoing financial obligations, putting the burden on owners to pay regardless of whether their units are fit for habitation.  

"Like others, I'm frustrated with paying HOA fees while out of our unit due to the fire, but we are still an owner of a unit and the fees pay for insurance and maintenance of the building and property," Benson said in a statemwnt to Fox26. "It is our understanding that we are legally obligated to pay our fees as an owner."

The only way to avoid paying HOA fees is to sell, which is what some of the owners have already resorted to, with Arends looking to join their ranks as soon as her unit is rebuilt.

As of Wednesday, three units in the complex were listed for sale on Realtor.com, with one already under contract.

The hidden risks of HOA membership

As homeowners associations become increasingly common across the U.S., Bayfront Towers owners' ordeal serves as a cautionary tale.

HOAs do offer benefits, with the association often covering landscaping, snow and trash removal services, as well as the upkeep and repair of common areas like swimming pools and security gates. But there are also potential downsides buyers should be aware of before signing on the dotted line. 

Mandatory HOA fees cover services and amenities whether an individual owner uses them or not, and strict bylaws may dictate exterior paint colors, home renovations, and even pet ownership.

Owners also have to be prepared to open their wallets for special assessments if the HOA reserve fund runs too low to undertake major unexpected repairs. 

HOAs are on the rise

According to recent Realtor.com data, the share of listings with HOA feels reached 43.6% in 2025, up from 41.9% the year. Condos and townhomes are more likely to have HOAs than single-family homes, and new builds are more likely to have HOAs than existing homes.

Regionally, Sun Belt states dominate in HOA prevalence, with Nevada leading the pack with over 68% of listings.

At the metro level, Las Vegas has the highest level of HOA participation topping 60%, followed by Orlando, FL (56.4%), and Houston (55..3%).

title: YouTubers Cody Ko and Kelsey Kreppel Slash Price of ‘Enchanting’ Malibu Compound Shortly After Welcoming Second Child
author: Hannah Chambers
preview: The home, which once belonged to Reese Witherspoon, has been reduced in price following the birth of the couple's second child.
summary_raw: The home, which once belonged to Reese Witherspoon, has been reduced in price following the birth of the couple's second child.
content_encoded_raw:
YouTube creators Cody Ko and Kelsey Kreppel are looking to offload Cranberry Ranch, their funky Malibu estate and the former home of "Legally Blonde" actress Reese Witherspoon, for $7.5 million after a second price slash.

The listing proclaims the five-bedroom, four-bathroom property is now “an undeniable value,” with the price sitting nearly $1.8 million below the initial January 2026 asking of $9.28 million—making a quick pit stop at $7.99 million in May.

Ko and Kreppel purchased the eclectic abode—which had reportedly been used as a wedding venue by Meg Haney, the owner between Witherspoon and the YouTube couple—for $7.7 million in April 2023.

Ko and Kreppel gave fellow internet personality Enes Yilmazer a tour of the compound over the summer, pointing out some of their favorite corners of the home and providing insight to their quirky design choices.

“This place is really enchanting,” said Ko, who named the property with his wife. “When you drive in, you feel the energy of the trees, and it feels like you’re in a storybook or something.”

A long private driveway leads to the 4,170-square-foot home, which sits on an 1.86-acre lot that hosts a variety of interesting additions: a detached all-glass gym, an outdoor sauna, a cold plunge, a hot tub, a permanent Airstream guest quarters, a chicken coop, a bocce court, and horse stables with a riding area.

The interior is just as eclectic, and as Ko explained, they wanted “to make it as funky as possible,” working with Los Angeles design studio Proem to bring the vision to life.

A light-flooded living room area was designed around a large, low-profile purple couch the couple admit they “spent way too much money” on before they even moved in, but looks right at home alongside a graphic, furry rug and a tiled propane fireplace.

The living room opens to a formal dining space the YouTubers often used for entertaining, opting to enjoy most of their meals as a family at a breakfast nook just under a window boasting picturesque views in the nearby kitchen.

At first glance, the kitchen appears to be among the more neutral spaces of the home. But upon closer inspection, the countertops are a muted rainbow onyx.

The primary bedroom stays connected to its peaceful Malibu surroundings with easy access to the backyard, and it's defined with a vaulted ceiling and ample windows. The primary bathroom features a double vanity, stained-glass windows, and a funky floral tub.

The nursery is a color-splashed bedroom, where pastel-hued walls and built-ins contrast against the dark, heated hardwood flooring found throughout the home.

Ko's recording studio is a highlight of the space, and will be recognizable to followers as the backdrop of his most-viewed videos.

“I want to make this look like no other studio I’ve ever been to,” he said, pointing to the “crazy” blue carpeting, “Minecraft” couch, and purple ceilings.

“I do everything in here. I spend all day long in here,” Ko added, explaining that he typically shoots up to two YouTube videos and makes music each day. In the corner, there’s a custom DJ booth. The space also includes a bathroom.

A fully-renovated barn on the property “is a social place,” where the couple primarily host gatherings. It features multiple “hangout zones,” with a king-size bed tucked away in the loft and additional spots to crash—such as a pull-out couch and a Murphy bed—scattered around the space.

The barn features a lounge and a full kitchen with a sizable island for hosting.

“We wanted people to come here and not feel like they have to drive an hour home,” said Kreppel.

Although the space is bursting with their personalities, they’ve begun to outgrow it as their family expands. Ko and Kreppel welcomed a son, Otis, in January 2024. Their second child—whose name and gender have yet to be revealed—arrived in June 2026.

In the YouTube house tour, Ko noted that despite the ample square footage of the home, much of it lies within the detached spaces, such as his recording space and the barn.

“It’s not, like, livable space for babies or toddlers,” he said, adding that the family also hopes to move closer to Kreppel’s parents.

The couple have enjoyed transforming the property, but are ready to pass it along for new people to appreciate.

“We feel like we can find something and make it our own again elsewhere,” said Kreppel.

title: $19 Million HOA Fees? The Devastating Assessments Crushing California Condo Owners
author: Natasha Etzel
preview: Condo owners in California are being hit with special assessment fees—from $26,000 to $19 million—with few ways to fight back.
summary_raw: Condo owners in California are being hit with special assessment fees—from $26,000 to $19 million—with few ways to fight back.
content_encoded_raw:
What would you do if you received an unexpected $26,000 HOA bill?

Residents of the Vilamoura condominium complex in San Clemente, CA, are facing that exact dilemma. The condo owners were recently hit with a $26,000 special assessment for roof replacement.

The residents were given three options: Pay in full, split it into two payments, or pay around $2,000 a month for six months, then $400 a month until the balance is paid off.

The condo owners argue that the HOA labeled it an emergency assessment, a designation they say is inaccurate because the association had long known the roofs needed repairs.

And this sort of issue keeps popping up. Over in Torrance, CA, residents were hit with assessments of more than $49,000 each to help pay for sweeping repairs to their condominium complex, ABC7 reports.

The 499-unit property is facing at least $19 million in work, including a $13 million overhaul of the building’s podium, along with repiping and elevator repairs.

Special assessments can hit any homeowner living in an HOA community. Knowing your options can help you make a more informed choice about how to cover the bill and minimize fees.

Your HOA may offer a payment plan

A special assessment is an extra fee that homeowners must pay when their HOA doesn't have enough money in reserves to cover major repairs or unexpected expenses. Depending on the size of the bill, paying in full may not be feasible, even if you have a sizable emergency fund.

John Donikian, vice president of Best Interest Financial and a home financing loan officer, recommends first checking whether your HOA offers an installment payment plan.

“If your HOA offers reasonable payment terms, you may be able to pay the assessment without taking out a new loan,” he explains.

Erik Leland, a real estate broker with Realty First and treasurer and secretary of Mountain Park HOA, the second-largest association in Oregon, says payment plans are common for larger special assessments but less common for smaller bills.

“Associations want assessments paid as quickly as possible, but they realize on really large bills that not offering a payment plan would lead to a wave of foreclosures and a loss of property value," he says.

Payment plans vary by association.

“They can range from payment plans that span 12 months to up to five years. The monthly amount is set by the board and then added to the regular dues,” says Leland. The HOA’s governing documents outline the interest rate. For his association, interest is 7%.

Leland also recommends verifying that your HOA followed the correct process. He says most associations can't charge a special assessment by board vote alone. His association requires a membership vote, and two-thirds of the members must vote in favor of the special assessment for it to be approved.

“If you get hit with a special assessment, confirm the process was actually followed. If steps were skipped, it can be challenged,” he says.

Homeowners who challenge a special assessment should know that they're still responsible for payment while the dispute is ongoing.

What happens if you don’t pay

If a homeowner misses a payment, the consequences can escalate quickly.

The specifics vary by state, but as Leland explains, in Oregon, a homeowner's account enters delinquency after 30 days. At that point, fees and interest start accumulating. The association will then issue a demand letter, giving the homeowner another 30 days to pay or enter into a payment plan.

“If they still do not respond, the association sends it to their law firm for collection. Once the law firm has it, fees start accumulating much faster. The whole process from delinquency to the eventual lawsuit can happen in months.”

Communication is key.

“The moment an owner realizes they might not be able to pay, they should call the association manager and open a dialog. The worst outcomes come from the people who ignore it at the start,” he says.

Homeowners who are worried they may fall behind on payments should ask their association about its hardship policy, as some HOAs may offer extended payment plans or case-by-case accommodations.

“Regardless of how you handle it, engage with the association before it goes to the lawyers, or there will be a lot more fees to pay that you cannot get rid of,” Leland adds.

How to finance what you can’t pay out of pocket

Donikian says the ideal financing solution depends on your equity, credit profile, and how quickly you need the money.

“If you need outside financing, look into a HELOC or home equity loan first if you have enough equity,” he explains.

Homeowners who don’t have at least 15% to 20% equity in their homes may want to consider an unsecured personal loan instead. But rates are typically higher than secured loans.

He cautions against a cash-out refinance: “I’d be hesitant to recommend refinancing your entire mortgage to pay for a special assessment, especially if your first-mortgage rate is low.”

Homeowners should also think twice about reaching for a credit card.

“It’s very tempting just to use a credit card and forget about the assessment, but that can quickly turn one large expense into several expensive payments,” Donikian adds.

How to prepare before getting a big HOA bill

Special assessments are a possibility when you own a condo or home in an HOA community. To be prepared, Donikian suggests homeowners keep extra money in an emergency reserve, especially in an older building or community. Staying aware of your association's financial health is also important.

“Keep an eye on the HOA’s financial statements, reserve study, meeting minutes, and special assessment history,” says Donikian. “Those documents can give you an idea of when major repairs will be needed and if your HOA has the reserves to cover the costs.”

For those considering a home in an HOA community, Leland recommends reviewing the reserve study before buying.

“You want reserves funded to at least 70%,” he says. “A low reserve percentage with no plan to fix it worries me. That means a special assessment is likely if anything goes wrong.”

Erik Leland , a real estate broker with Realty First and treasurer and secretary of Mountain Park HOA, the second-largest association in Oregon, says payment plans are common for larger special assessments but less common for smaller bills. “Associations want assessments paid as quickly as possible, but they realize on really large bills that not offering a payment plan would lead to a wave of foreclosures and a loss of property value," he says. Payment plans vary by association. “They can range from payment plans that span 12 months to up to five years. The monthly amount is set by the board and then added to the regular dues,” says Leland. The HOA’s governing documents outline the interest rate. For his association, interest is 7%. Leland also recommends verifying that your HOA followed the correct process. He says most associations can't charge a special assessment by board vote alone. His association requires a membership vote, and two-thirds of the members must vote in favor of the special assessment for it to be approved. “If you get hit with a special assessment, confirm the process was actually followed. If steps were skipped, it can be challenged,” he says. Homeowners who challenge a special assessment should know that they're still responsible for payment while the dispute is ongoing. What happens if you don’t pay If a homeowner misses a payment, the consequences can escalate quickly. The specifics vary by state, but as Leland explains, in Oregon, a homeowner's account enters delinquency after 30 days. At that point, fees and interest start accumulating. The association will then issue a demand letter, giving the homeowner another 30 days to pay or enter into a payment plan. “If they still do not respond, the association sends it to their law firm for collection. Once the law firm has it, fees start accumulating much faster. The whole process from delinquency to the eventual lawsuit can happen in months.” Communication is key. “The moment an owner realizes they might not be able to pay, they should call the association manager and open a dialog. The worst outcomes come from the people who ignore it at the start,” he says. Homeowners who are worried they may fall behind on payments should ask their association about its hardship policy, as some HOAs may offer extended payment plans or case-by-case accommodations. “Regardless of how you handle it, engage with the association before it goes to the lawyers, or there will be a lot more fees to pay that you cannot get rid of,” Leland adds. How to finance what you can’t pay out of pocket Donikian says the ideal financing solution depends on your equity, credit profile, and how quickly you need the money. “If you need outside financing, look into a HELOC or home equity loan first if you have enough equity,” he explains. Homeowners who don’t have at least 15% to 20% equity in their homes may want to consider an unsecured personal loan instead. But rates are typically higher than secured loans. He cautions against a cash-out refinance: “I’d be hesitant to recommend refinancing your entire mortgage to pay for a special assessment, especially if your first-mortgage rate is low.” Homeowners should also think twice about reaching for a credit card. “It’s very tempting just to use a credit card and forget about the assessment, but that can quickly turn one large expense into several expensive payments,” Donikian adds. How to prepare before getting a big HOA bill Special assessments are a possibility when you own a condo or home in an HOA community. To be prepared, Donikian suggests homeowners keep extra money in an emergency reserve, especially in an older building or community. Staying aware of your association's financial health is also important. “Keep an eye on the HOA’s financial statements, reserve study, meeting minutes, and special assessment history,” says Donikian. “Those documents can give you an idea of when major repairs will be needed and if your HOA has the reserves to cover the costs.” For those considering a home in an HOA community, Leland recommends reviewing the reserve study before buying. “You want reserves funded to at least 70%,” he says. “A low reserve percentage with no plan to fix it worries me. That means a special assessment is likely if anything goes wrong.” ​

title: A South Carolina Man Planted a Garden in His Yard—Now His Town Is Taking Him to Court
author: Eric Goldschein
preview: A South Carolina town wants a resident to cut down a new pollinator garden.
summary_raw: A South Carolina town wants a resident to cut down a new pollinator garden.
content_encoded_raw:
Rich Ashford, an arborist and relative newcomer to the town of Cowpens, SC, is going to court over his garden. 

The conflict stems from a dispute about the height of what Ashford is growing in his front yard. Town ordinances say that the yard is overgrown, while Ashford contends that his garden qualifies for an exception for “cultivated gardens.” He says his property is a state-recognized natural wildlife habitat. 

Though the town ordinance is clear, legal experts think Ashford has a pretty good chance to beat the case—or that the town will need to change how it polices this issue.

A native solution to a landscaping headache

Ashford originally had no plans to become a homeowner in the town of Cowpens, but the Ohio native bought a house on the town’s main street back in 2020. 

“I got tricked by this big, beautiful Victorian home,” he tells Realtor.com®. “I got a smoking deal on this old Victorian house that was in really, really bad condition and had been neglected for 30-plus years.”

Ashford, in his telling, has become a well-known part of the community in the small town over the past few years. He left his career in banking soon after arriving in the town to pursue arborist work full time, with an emphasis on working with the land. 

“It's ecosystems, it's natives, it's xeriscaping, it's using what you have at your disposal as opposed to trying to force a yard to look like a certain thing,” he says. 

His emphasis on native plants and wanting “nature to do its thing” is part of what led him to approach his own yard differently. The previous owner, Ashford says, had covered the front yard in pea gravel and displayed tombstones there. As a result, when he bought the property, the soil was “trash.”

He filled the area with mulch, but everything that grew in failed to hold the topsoil, which would wash away in the rain and create mud and mess. 

“So what do I do? Easy solution: what grows in ground where other stuff doesn't grow? … natives,” he says. 

Ashford had previously experimented with natives in his backyard to some success, and he decided to plant an “Upland Meadows” mix from Ernst Conservation—a native seed producer—along with a wildflower and pollinator butterfly garden mix, between his two water oak trees out front.

A pollinator garden takes hold

The resulting growth included grasses, native oats, and blooming flowers. Quickly, the garden was attracting pollinators and wildlife that the old yard never could. 

“I get lots of pollinators, lots of butterflies out front, bees of all varieties. We're starting to get some migratory birds,” Ashford says.

It also attracted the attention of his neighbors. Ashford was prepared for pushback in a town where most people tend to plant flowers more conservatively—not ”tall grass and these weird flowers,” as he described it—but says that’s not what he got. 

“We had a town yard sale in May, and a bunch of people came by and told me how much they liked what I had done out front. I had a couple clients in town who said the same, and so you know, I sort of gave up on anybody saying anything,” he says. 

Where he did get pushback was from the town administrator, Steve Bolin.

In May, Ashford received a citation saying that his garden was in violation of a town ordinance. In a subsequent call with Bolin, Ashford says he was told the pollinator garden was the issue, as parts of it had grown above 12 inches. 

Ashford says he offered Bolin a planting list of what was in his yard, and that he believed what he planted and how he planted it met the exception of a cultivated garden. Soon after, a court summons arrived. Ashford’s court date is Sept. 17, 2026. 

Bolin did not respond to requests for comment from Realtor.com. Meanwhile, the town mayor, Jarred Spencer, told local newspaper The Post and Courier that enforcement of the ordinance is happening here because “people are complaining.”

The bones of a strong legal case

Ashford feels confident in representing himself in court and that he will avoid the fines the town wants to levy on him. 

“I have my rights, and you're not going to tell me I can't do something that the law says I can do,” he says. 

On one hand the ordinance seems clear. On the other hand, the exception properly muddles it. So where does that leave this case?

“The town of Cowpens has the right to require homeowners to maintain their property. Someone can't just stop mowing an overgrown lawn and call it a garden to skirt responsibility for it,” says Colin Ram, an attorney in South Carolina. “The problem is that the reported facts fit the ordinance's exception unusually well. Ashford apparently bought specific seed mixes, planted them in a defined area between two trees, and continues to mow the grass around it. Under the town's own logic, that's a hard thing to distinguish from a cultivated garden.”

Ram says the town could struggle to answer the question of, “If this isn't a cultivated garden, what counts as one?” He also notes that the town may be prosecuting this case while missing the bigger picture. 

“In 2025, the South Carolina General Assembly adopted a resolution encouraging local governments and private landowners to use native plants in landscaping to support pollinators. The resolution isn't binding law and doesn't decide this case, but it's hard to miss the contrast between South Carolina lawmakers encouraging this kind of native planting while the Town of Cowpens is prosecuting a homeowner for it,” Ram says. 

Another attorney, Edward Susolik, president of Callahan & Blaine, a firm that handles real estate litigation cases, says that though Ashford’s dictionary definition is a “great sound bite,” the judge’s decision will likely come down to evidence of planting that is “intentional and maintained significantly.” But he also thinks that the most elegant solution won’t require a court ruling.

“These kinds of issues typically get resolved when the municipality establishes a clear standard and does not leave anything up to interpretation through vague terminology like 'cultivated.’” says Susolik. “Cowpens could [create] a percentage requirement, a list of acceptable plants, or an advance registration system for planting native plants.”

What comes next?

Ashford is gearing up for his case. He says he plans to attend the hearing, bringing his credentials and even a proposal for a revised ordinance that would define pollinator gardens. He believes that he may be fined $500 a day for his garden if he loses the case. 

“I’m gonna go down swinging,” Ashford says. “If I have to cut it down, I gotta cut it down. If I have to come out here as a ruler and cut it 12 inches. I guess I'll do that.” 

While it’s possible the case is dropped or dismissed, Ashford says, he’s prepared for any outcome, as well as for what comes after it.

“If you think I'm just gonna take this, and become some like, ridiculously compliant citizen because I'm scared of the town of Cowpens, you are out of your mind,” he says. “And if I have to start embarrassing people in public, I'm gonna start embarrassing people in public.”

title: NBA Star Giannis Antetokounmpo Picks Up $13.5 Million Florida Mansion—Months After Miami Heat Trade
author: Kelsi Karruli
preview: The basketball icon has put down roots in the Sunshine State, months after being traded from the Millwaukee Bucks.
summary_raw: The basketball icon has put down roots in the Sunshine State, months after being traded from the Millwaukee Bucks.
content_encoded_raw:
Basketball star Giannis Antetokounmpo has snapped up a lavish abode in South Florida after being traded to Miami Heat.

The 31-year-old forward was traded to the Florida-based team in June, along with Bobby Portis. In return, the Bucks will get Tyler Herro, Kel'el Ware, Jaime Jaquez Jr., Kasparas Jakucionis, three first-round picks, one pick swap and one second-rounder, as first reported by ESPN.

Now, it appears as though the athlete—who was traded from the Millwaukee Bucks is putting down roots in the Sunshine State, having dribbled his way to a $13.5 million mansion in Pinecrest, as first reported by The Real Deal.

The 12,000-square-foot property comes comes with eight bedrooms, 10 bathrooms, two half-bathrooms, a media room, a resort-style pool, and a Jacuzzi.

The dwelling, which was built in 2026, also sits on a 1.06-acre lot, as per the listing.

Just one day before news of the trade was announced, Antetokounmpo found himself at the center of mounting speculation about his future in the NBA.

Sources had told ESPN that the he would be bidding farewell to Wisconsin, with discussions surrounding his future reportedly gaining steam ahead of the NBA Draft on June 23 and June 24.

According to the outlet, Antetokounmpo was in serious talks with both the Boston and Miami-based teams, and it was reported that he was likely to be traded before the draft event began.

The Boston Celtics reportedly proposed swapping five-time All-Star Jaylen Brown for Antetokounmpo, while the Miami Heat is said to have offered cost-controlled contracts.

Trade rumors surrounding Antetokounmpo have intensified over the past year as the superstar reportedly became disillusioned with Milwaukee's trajectory.

ESPN reported that after trade-deadline discussions failed to resolve concerns, the relationship further deteriorated when Antetokounmpo raised questions about the team's decision to sideline him late in the season due to a knee injury.

His move to the Heat marks a significant milestone in his NBA career—which began with the Bucks in 2013—and has raised many questions about his future in the sport, debate that extends beyond his performance on the court.

Among the questions raised by the trade chatter is what might become of the sprawling Milwaukee home he has owned during his rise to NBA superstardom.

title: Nicolas Cage’s $10.5 Million Malibu Mansion Threatened by Massive 30-Foot Sinkhole After Driveway Collapses
author: Kelsi Karruli
preview: Just two years after the actor snapped up the modern home, shocking images have revealed extensive damage outside the residence.
summary_raw: Just two years after the actor snapped up the modern home, shocking images have revealed extensive damage outside the residence.
content_encoded_raw:
Actor Nicolas Cage's lavish Malibu mansion is facing a dramatic threat after a massive hole opened up where part of the property's driveway once stood.

Just two years after the 62-year-old actor snapped up the modern 4,000-square-foot home, shocking images have revealed extensive damage outside the residence, with the collapse cracking open the sidewalk and leaving behind a gaping hole.

Large chunks of concrete could be seen scattered around and inside the collapsed area, while orange traffic cones cordoned off the site as workers surveyed the damage.

According to KTLA, firefighters responded to the property on Tuesday following reports of a gas main break.

A public information officer told the local news outlet that the roughly 30-foot-by-30-foot hole was caused by "coastal erosion."

The gas company remained at the scene as crews worked to restore the damaged gas main.

Despite the scale of the collapse, KTLA reported that no evacuations were ordered and no injuries were reported.

No one appeared to be inside the mansion when the hole opened up, and the residence itself appeared to be undergoing work at the time.

“As a matter of fact, the house looks like it is under some sort of renovation,” KTLA reporter Rich Prickett noted.

The ocean-facing abode, which comes with a secluded beach and a rare roof deck, first appeared on the market in March of that year for $11.25 million, according to Realtor.com®. However, the waterfront residence had also been simultaneously offered for rent for $25,000 a month.

The property comes complete with a private courtyard and a two-car garage that has an elevator. The living room, bathed in natural light, offers vaulted ceilings, a chic bar area, and a fireplace.

Floor-to-ceiling glass walls and sliding doors seamlessly connect indoor and outdoor spaces, such as ocean-facing decks and a rare rooftop space.

On the second level, a chef's kitchen with high-end stainless appliances, a center island, and sweeping ocean views is poised to inspire impressive culinary endeavors.

The third floor features four en suite bedrooms, along with a primary bedroom facing the Pacific Ocean, with a spa-worthy bath, fireplace, and an ocean-facing deck.

In addition to the home's beach frontage, the property includes an adjacent beach lot.

Prior to that purchase, Cage faced troubles with an infamous "haunted" mansion situated in New Orleans' French Quarter.

In 2009, the actor lost the property to foreclosure, and it was subsequently purchased by Regions Bank for $4.5 million.

The following year, the home was sold to an investor for $2.1 million.

Before that March 2024 listing, the property had bounced on and off the market multiple times since the summer of 2022 and had once been offered for as much as $17.9 million.

By comparison, Cage seems to have secured an impressive deal—although, judging by the success of his most recent on-screen endeavor, paying the full ask might not have been out of the question for him.

The actor and producer recently appeared in the horror film "Longlegs," which became the "highest grossing independent film of the year," with $100 million at the box office, according to Variety.

The "Face/Off" star is known to keep a full-time residence in Nevada, the site of his iconic movies, "Leaving Las Vegas" and "Honeymoon in Vegas." But now, when the 60-year-old yearns for the Pacific, he can land in this newly purchased perch.

Cage has traded real estate in California before.

In fact, he owned a San Francisco Queen Anne Victorian, which he picked up in 1989 and held for 16 years. He sold the property some 20 years ago but left behind personal touches, such as custom stained-glass windows.

In March, he reportedly snapped up a sprawling two-bedroom condo in the heart of Manhattan for $6.5 million—and took out a $4.55 million mortgage for the deal.

The actor is said to have purchased the unit inside the coveted Essex House Residences building at 160 Central Park South for a steep $1.4 million discount—after the property initially hit the market for $7.9 million.

The home measures across 2,400 square feet and is a combination of two units, as first reported by The Real Deal.

The double-sized unit was described in its listing as offering "an unparalleled blend of elegance, comfort, and convenience, right at the doorstep of Central Park," with its staggering views of the iconic Manhattan site noted as one of its most alluring attributes.

Cage will likely feel right at home inside Essex House, which has played host to a slew of famous faces over the years, including the late actor and musician David Bowie and his wife, Iman.

Oasis star Liam Gallagher also purchased a pad in the unit in 2012, selling it two years later.

title: Homebuyers Shift to Riskier Mortgages as Interest Rates Rise
author: Julie Gerstein
preview: Applications for adjustable rate mortgages are up week over week, as buyers look for interest rate relief.
summary_raw: Applications for adjustable rate mortgages are up week over week, as buyers look for interest rate relief.
content_encoded_raw:
Mortgage applications dipped this past week as rising interest rates and persistent market pressures kept some buyers out of the market and pushed others toward riskier loan structures.

For the week ending Sept. 4, the Mortgage Bankers Association's Market Composite Index—a measure of total mortgage loan application volume—fell 2.7% on a seasonally adjusted basis from the previous week.

“Higher mortgage rates continue to weigh on prospective homebuyers looking to act, even as housing inventory has increased in many markets,” said Joel Kan, MBA’s vice president and deputy chief economist

Meanwhile, the Purchase Index, a leading indicator for home sales, decreased 0.2% week over week on a seasonally adjusted basis, and was down 4% from a year earlier. Refinance activity fell 6% week over week and was down 25% year over year.

The mortgage application slowdown corresponds with rising interest rates. This week, MBA says 30-year fixed rate hit 6.85%, up from 6.79%, the highest since June 2025 and 36 basis points higher than a year ago. Thirty-year jumbo loans have climbed to 7.08%, the highest they've been since July 2024.

These rates have pushed a growing number of buyers toward riskier adjustable-rate mortgages, Kan said.

Adjustable-rate mortgages (ARMs) are considered riskier because monthly payments can vary sharply after the initial low-interest-rate period ends. Maturing ARMs were widely blamed for the 2008 housing bust and subsequent recession.

"Purchase applications overall were little changed from last week, but more borrowers have shifted to using ARM loans, with the ARM share of applications at 8.5%, the highest share since June," Kan said. "Higher mortgage rates continue to weigh on prospective homebuyers looking to act, even as housing inventory has increased in many markets."

As 30-year-fixed rates climbed, ARM rates fell to 5.82% from 5.94% last week.

How mortgage rates are calculated

Mortgage rates are calculated based on various factors in the economy, and the length of your loan and credit score will also factor into the mortgage rate you qualify for.

The 30-year mortgage rate is tied to the yield of the 10-year Treasury note, because most 30-year mortgages are either paid off or refinanced in roughly eight to 11 years.

That makes the duration on the loans roughly comparable, and mortgage lenders use the 10-year Treasury as a benchmark for setting rates, adding on a risk premium.

Long-term yields for Treasury notes are determined by a number of factors, including the supply of and demand for U.S. government debt, and investor expectations for inflation over the life of the bonds.

title: Joanna Gaines Gets Real About ‘Grieving’ Missed Time with Her Children to Focus on Her Growing Business
author: Hannah Chambers
preview: The HGTV star opened up about the challenge of balancing work and motherhood, sharing an emotional conversation with daughter, Ella.
summary_raw: The HGTV star opened up about the challenge of balancing work and motherhood, sharing an emotional conversation with daughter, Ella.
content_encoded_raw:
HGTV star Joanna Gaines is an expert in all things home design, but when it comes to parenting, she’s still learning every single day.

During an appearance on “Joy 101 with Hoda Kotb,” the mother of five got real about a tender moment she recently experienced with her oldest daughter, 19-year-old Ella Rose Gaines.

At the helm of a home and lifestyle empire, Joanna always seems to have her hands full with new projects. And as she prepared to send her second child away to college, she started to worry that she hadn’t balanced it all quite as well as she hoped to.

“Mom guilt never goes away. It’s something you have to manage,” said Joanna, 48, before recalling an honest conversation she had while driving Ella to the airport.

“I remember crying a little bit and thinking, ‘OK, this is the moment I can just say I’m sorry for anywhere I wasn’t present,’” she recalled. “For months, what I was grieving was, ‘I wasn’t home the whole time.’”

Explaining that she was a “stay at home mom for a portion” of Ella’s childhood, Joanna feared she missed out on key moments as her professional life started to ramp up.

“I held that mom guilt of, is she thinking I wasn’t there enough?” she shared.

The “Fixer Upper” co-host went on to explain that she had created a “narrative” in which she assumed Ella had felt a certain way about her parenting, worrying she had spent too much time working.

Joanna offered an apology to Ella, hoping to have a “beautiful” moment of forgiveness. She was shocked when her daughter “kind of got mad” in response.

“She got upset and said, ‘Mom, are you serious? All you’ve taught me is I can do everything and anything,’” Joanna said.

“The narrative she’s built up over the years is not the mom guilt that I’ve been holding,” the Waco, TX champion continued. “Instead, it’s one of strength and empowerment and beauty.”

Joanna described the moment as “life changing,” and from it, realized that it’s best to have conversations about these types of feelings.

“I should have brought that up three years ago,” she said.

While it seems as though Joanna is grateful for the learning experience, she still has a wealth of knowledge to share with fellow parents who may be looking to her for advice.

The entrepreneur recently shared some words of wisdom with fellow parents of college-bound young adults, drawing on her experiences sending both Ella, and her firstborn—21-year-old Drake Gaines—off to start their next chapters.

“To all the parents sending their kids off to college… I know that feeling all too well,” Joanna wrote in an emotional Aug. 16 Instagram post.

“I’ve been on that side of move-in day… as hard as that goodbye is, there’s nothing more fulfilling than watching your kid grow beyond you—it’s one of the greatest gifts of being a parent,” she continued. “May you find joy, comfort, and gratitude in letting go.”

Joanna shared the sweet sentiment alongside a series of family photos, showcasing hugs, graduation caps, and packed suitcases.

Although Joanna and husband Chip Gaines, 51, often remark on their parenting journeys, they have largely kept their kids out of the spotlight since 2018. In addition to Ella and Drake, the couple are parents to Duke, 18, Emmie, 16, and Crew, 8.

The family has previously shared that Drake is pursuing a degree in business entrepreneurship at Mary Hardin-Baylor in Belton, TX, and that Ella is continuing her education at an undisclosed institution “across the country.”

It’s unclear what kind of a degree Ella is working towards, but she’s already boasting an impressive design resume. She joined her parents for a spinoff show, “Fixer Upper: Colorado Mountain House,” in which she put her skills to the test and owned a project.

title: Data Center Boom Triggers Homeowner Fears Over Skyrocketing Electric Costs
author: Tristan Navera
preview: Agents and their clients are worried data centers will drive up utility costs. But their impact on property values is less clear.
summary_raw: Agents and their clients are worried data centers will drive up utility costs. But their impact on property values is less clear.
content_encoded_raw:
Real estate agents and their clients are worried data centers will drive up utility costs. But their impact on property values is less clear, the National Association of Realtors® found.

About 61% of NAR members said their clients were concerned that data centers would raise energy costs, and 56% reported concerns about water usage, according to survey data released on Wednesday.

As well, 43% feared environmental contamination and 32% feared the impact on the immediate landscape.

However, opinions on the impact on home values were divided. About 25% of agents surveyed expected data centers to have a positive impact on residential values, while 22% perceived a negative impact.

“There is no single data center effect. Instead, the story varies significantly depending on the local market,” said NAR Chief Economist Lawrence Yun. “The number of data centers alone does not tell us what will happen to home values, jobs, or utility costs.”

The data tracks with recent Realtor.com research on data centers. The research found data centers are moving into increasingly rural areas. While they do affect property taxes, the impact on the average homeowner's tax burden is complicated. And while the separate study from Realtor.com found no impact on property values, that data tracks only large facilities in the two years after they open.

Data centers have emerged as a flashpoint in the 2026 midterms. Surveys show data centers are unpopular with the public, and lawmakers are weighing how to regulate the industry and its impacts on energy prices, the environment, and the real estate market.

Counties with more data centers do tend to have higher home values, NAR found. Those with 10 or more data centers have a median home value of $431,750 versus $174,500 for counties without a data center. Those with data center concentrations saw their home values jump 95% from 2014 to 2024. Counties without data centers saw their values jump just 64%.

"This does not mean that data centers caused home values to rise," the report states. "Counties with more data centers also tend to have higher incomes, younger populations and more college educated residents. All these factors are also associated with stronger housing demand."

Data and perceptions

NAR looked at data center activity across 3,200 counties, comparing employment, housing characteristics, and electricity costs. It also conducted a survey of real estate agents working in those cities. The group tracked 1,474 data center projects in 251 counties. About 92% of those counties have no data centers. Meanwhile, 34 counties have 10 or more.

But those projects are largely concentrated in just a few areas: Almost 19% of the data centers NAR found are just in Northern Virginia's "data center alley" in Loudoun and Prince William counties. Meanwhile, 75 data centers are in California's Santa Clara County and 63 are in Arizona's Maricopa County. NAR found those markets attract data centers because of available land and power infrastructure.

Household incomes tend to be higher in counties with data centers, with a median household income of about $89,000 in counties that have 10 or more data centers, versus $64,000 in counties without them. Realtor.com research found that data center developments, though, are shifting away from these large metro areas and into increasingly rural places.

NAR did find that the presence of data centers is associated with faster growth of residential electricity rates. But having more data centers didn't cause steeper growth. And counties with the most data centers don't have the highest residential electricity rates.

“We do not see evidence of weaker housing markets in counties with a large data center presence,” Yun said. “But these are county-level numbers, and they can’t tell us what happens to an individual home next to a facility. That’s why local knowledge and credible data matter so much right now.”

Agents' attitudes split

The NAR member survey found different viewpoints on data centers, which could vary by region.

About 38% of agents in the survey reported a data center proposed or in place in their local market.

NAR found markets in the West had stronger optimism that residential property values would rise with data centers.

Among five key sentiments in the survey, Realtors found residents are strongly opposed, but some see them as inevitable or necessary infrastructure.

They are likely to create tax revenue but could also strain local power grids. Meanwhile, the study urges that real estate agents "need to be informed from a credible source about the impact."
